eFAST is notoriously unreliable for assessing the retroperitoneum; CT is the gold standard for that space.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): Summary box 29.5 Utilisation of eFAST... Cannot reliably exclude injury in penetrating trauma... Is unreliable for assessment of the retroperitoneum

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A 78-year-old patient with progressive neurological deterioration undergoes a CT brain. The scan reveals a diffuse concave hypodense lesion overlying the brain surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Diffuse axonal injury
Cerebral contusion
Acute subdural haematoma
Chronic subdural haematoma
Acute extradural haematoma
correctOption: Chronic subdural haematoma
optionExplanations: DAI is often poorly visualized on CT, sometimes showing small hemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum, but is best seen on MRI.
Contusions appear heterogeneous, containing a mix of blood and injured brain matter, typically near irregular bone.
Acute subdural hematomas are hyperdense (bright white) because they contain fresh blood.
Chronic subdurals appear hypodense (darker than brain) because the blood has degraded and liquified over days or weeks.
Extradural hematomas are hyperdense and lentiform (biconvex) because they are constrained by dural attachments.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 367 (Book Page): Summary box 28.8 Chronic subdural haemorrhage... Diffuse hypodense lesion on CT... Page 366 (Book Page): subdural blood is free to expand across the brain surface, giving a difuse concave appearance.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: Why might a plain radiograph of the pelvis fail to show an obvious fracture in a patient who has a significant pelvic ring disruption?
options: The vast majority of suspected pelvic fractures are only visible on MRI
Radiographs are only indicated for Type A Tile classification injuries
The pelvic ring is immensely strong and cannot be fractured in more than one place
Pelvic hemorrhage creates a 'ground-glass' appearance that obscures bone lines
The patient likely has a pelvic binder in place which has reduced the fracture
correctOption: The patient likely has a pelvic binder in place which has reduced the fracture
optionExplanations: MRI is rarely used acutely; CT is the definitive modality for stable patients, but plain films are standard screening.
Type A injuries are stable; radiographs are crucial for identifying unstable Type B and C injuries.
The pelvic ring is circular and routinely gives way at more than one point when significant force is applied.
Hemorrhage can cause haziness but 'ground-glass' is not a typical pelvic X-ray term for blood; the mechanical reduction is the documented reason for false negatives.
Pelvic binders are designed to compress the pelvic volume; this mechanical reduction can hide fracture lines and symphyseal diastasis on a standard X-ray.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 384 (Book Page): It is important to note that the vast majority of patients with suspected pelvic fractures may have a pelvic binder in place and hence plain radiograph fndings may be normal.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: Which radiological finding on an erect chest radiograph is considered the most common suggesting traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
options: Presence of a fuid meniscus in the hemithorax
Deviated nasogastric tube
Tracheal deviation toward the side of injury
A widened mediastinum
Fracture of the frst and second ribs
correctOption: A widened mediastinum
optionExplanations: A fluid meniscus represents a hemothorax, which can accompany aortic injury but isn't specific to the vessel itself.
A deviated NG tube can occur but is not as common or definitive as the general mediastinal widening.
Tracheal deviation is more classically associated with tension pneumothorax (away) or lung collapse (toward).
Mediastinal widening is the most common and classic screening finding for aortic tears on plain films, though it is non-specific.
First and second rib fractures are high-energy markers associated with aortic injury but are skeletal findings, not the primary aortic sign.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum ( Figure 29.4 ).

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
coreConcept: Follow-up Imaging of Occult Scaphoid Fractures
statement: If a patient presents with pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox following a fall on the outstretched hand but initial radiographs are negative, what is the appropriate management?
options: Reassure the patient and allow full weight-bearing mobility
Perform a technetium-99 bone scan within the first 24 hours
Begin early active range of motion to prevent joint stiffness
Immobilise the wrist and repeat the radiographs 10–14 days later
Obtain an immediate CT scan to rule out a fracture definitively
correctOption: Immobilise the wrist and repeat the radiographs 10–14 days later
optionExplanations: Ignoring snuffbox tenderness risks missing a scaphoid fracture, leading to non-union and avascular necrosis.
Bone scans are sensitive but generally not the first-line 'standard protocol' compared to repeat plain films.
Early motion is contraindicated in suspected scaphoid fractures as it may impede healing of a non-displaced fracture.
Scaphoid fractures are often occult initially; bone resorption at the fracture site after 2 weeks makes them visible on repeat films.
While CT or MRI can be used early if resources allow, the 'standard protocol' described is clinical review and delayed repeat imaging.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 412 (Book Page): If a fracture is not evident on the initial radiographs and the patient remains tender in the anatomical snuff box, then treat as a suspected scaphoid fracture until a fracture is actively excluded. The standard protocol of a suspected scaphoid fracture is to immobilise the wrist and examine again 10–14 days later.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In the initial resuscitation of a severely injured patient with massive arterial bleeding from a limb wound, what is the immediate management priority according to the cABCDE protocol sequence?
options: Securing the airway with cervical spine control
Application of direct pressure and haemostatic dressings
Insertion of two large-bore intravenous cannulae
Administration of high-fow oxygen
Checking the Glasgow Coma Scale score
correctOption: Application of direct pressure and haemostatic dressings
optionExplanations: While airway (A) is a priority in standard ATLS, the modified cABCDE protocol places control of exsanguinating external haemorrhage (c) first to prevent immediate death from exsanguination.
Correct. In cases of massive external arterial bleeding, immediate control with packs, direct pressure, and haemostatic dressings is the first priority, even before airway management.

Circulation (C) comes after catastrophic haemorrhage control (c), Airway (A), and Breathing (B). Large-bore IV access is part of the general circulatory assessment, not the immediate first step for arterial bleeding.
Breathing (B) is assessed after catastrophic haemorrhage and airway. High-flow oxygen is vital but follows the arrest of life-threatening bleeding.
Disability (D) is assessed later in the primary survey after life-threatening bleeding, airway, and breathing have been addressed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): Experience from war zones over the past 20 years has shown that exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed... Bleeding must be controlled immediately by the application of packs and pressure directly onto the bleeding wound and proximal artery. Haemostatic dressings that contain agents that augment local coagulation are now available.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A 35-year-old male is undergoing initial fluid resuscitation for haemorrhagic shock. During the period of permissive hypotension, what is the target systolic blood pressure and what physiological rationale necessitates that this approach be strictly time-limited?
options: Target 70–90 mmHg; to prevent the development of fat embolism syndrome
Target >100 mmHg; to avoid the lethal triad of acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia
Target 60–80 mmHg; to prevent renal tubular necrosis
Target 90–110 mmHg; to ensure adequate cerebral perfusion in all polytrauma cases
Target 70–90 mmHg; to allow for identification and control of the haemorrhage source
correctOption: Target 70–90 mmHg; to allow for identification and control of the haemorrhage source
optionExplanations: Permissive hypotension is not directly related to the prevention of fat embolism syndrome, which usually occurs hours to days after long bone fractures.

Targeting high blood pressures (>100 mmHg) during active bleeding can cause 'popping the clot' and exacerbate coagulopathy; the lethal triad is avoided by early damage control, not by over-resuscitation with high BP targets.
The target range is 70–90 mmHg, not 60–80. While renal health is important, the primary rationale for the time limit is haemorrhage control.
A target of >90 mmHg is reserved specifically for suspected head injury, not all polytrauma cases, to ensure cerebral perfusion pressure.

Correct. Permissive hypotension targets a systolic BP of 70–90 mmHg (higher if head injury is suspected) to maintain vital organ perfusion while minimizing clot disruption. It is time-limited because the haemorrhage source must be controlled to prevent definitive shock progression.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): The initial aim of resuscitation is to maintain the blood supply to the vital organs... For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg... However, the key to this approach of permissive hypotension is that it is time limited. The primary source of haemorrhage must be identifed and controlled as soon as possible.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In the management of a blunt trauma patient suspected of significant haemorrhage, what is the specific dosing regimen for the administration of the antifibrinolytic agent Tranexamic acid (TXA)?
options: 1g given only if the systolic blood pressure drops below 90 mmHg
1g given over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over the next 8 hours
2g given as a rapid bolus within 3 hours of injury
10mg/kg administered every 8 hours for three doses
500mg given every 4 hours for the first 24 hours
correctOption: 1g given over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over the next 8 hours
optionExplanations: TXA should be given to any patient suspected of significant haemorrhage, specifically if systolic BP is <110 mmHg or pulse is >110 bpm, not just for BP <90 mmHg.
Correct. The CRASH-2 trial established the standard trauma dosing as 1g IV over 10 minutes followed by 1g IV infusion over 8 hours.
The total dose is 2g, but it is split into a loading dose and an infusion, not a single 2g rapid bolus.
Dosing is standardized at 1g/1g in trauma rather than weight-based dosing for adults in this acute protocol.
This is not a standard dosing protocol for acute trauma haemorrhage according to the source text.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid is an antifbrinolytic drug that reduces the risk of mortality from bleeding... One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A 28-year-old unrestrained driver is brought to the ED after a high-speed collision. He is hemodynamically unstable (BP 75/40 mmHg, HR 135 bpm) despite receiving 2 units of warmed O-negative blood. A FAST scan reveals massive free fluid in the abdomen. What is the most appropriate acute management plan?
options: Transfer immediately for Whole-Body CT (WBCT) to identify all injuries
Perform a diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) to confirm the FAST findings
Application of a pelvic binder and immediate MRI of the torso
Immediate transfer to the operating theatre for trauma laparotomy
Wait for cross-matched blood and achieve BP >120 mmHg before surgery
correctOption: Immediate transfer to the operating theatre for trauma laparotomy
optionExplanations: While WBCT is a gold standard, it is contraindicated in patients who remain hemodynamically unstable despite resuscitation; they require immediate surgical control.
DPL is redundant if FAST has already identified massive free fluid in an unstable patient.
A pelvic binder should be applied, but MRI has no role in acute trauma resuscitation due to time constraints and incompatibility with resuscitation equipment.

Correct. A patient with persistent instability and a positive FAST scan for intra-abdominal bleeding requires immediate operative haemorrhage control (laparotomy) before further diagnostic imaging like CT.
Resuscitation and surgery should happen concurrently; waiting to normalize BP in the face of active surgical bleeding is futile and dangerous.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Some patients will be so haemodynamically unstable on arrival that they need immediate surgical control of their haemorrhage before a CT scan. The most likely sources are abdominal or pelvic bleeding... A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: What specific physiological markers define the 'triad of death' that Damage Control Surgery (DCS) aims to avoid by limiting the initial operative time?
options: Hypocalcemia, hypertension, and bradycardia
Acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia
Uraemia, hyperkalaemia, and hypoxaemia
Hypernatremia, alkalosis, and tachycardia
Hyperglycemia, ketosis, and dehydration
correctOption: Acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia
optionExplanations: Cushing's triad (hypertension, bradycardia) is associated with raised ICP, not the lethal triad of general trauma.
Correct. Acidosis, coagulopathy, and hypothermia are the three components that reinforce each other, leading to irreversible physiological decline in severely injured patients.
These markers represent renal failure and respiratory failure but are not the primary components of the lethal triad defined in damage control principles.
The triad consists of acidosis (low pH), not alkalosis, and involves hypothermia, not simple tachycardia.
Hyperglycemia and ketosis are components of diabetic ketoacidosis, not the lethal triad of trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): Prolonged procedures result in additional trauma and further immune and physiological derangement; the ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A trauma patient has been resuscitated and is being considered for Early Total Care (ETC) of their long bone fractures. Which venous lactate level indicates that the patient is likely well-resuscitated and suitable for definitive surgical fixation?
options: Lactate <2 mmol/L
Lactate of 2.5 mmol/L with an upward trend
Lactate >5 mmol/L
Lactate between 4 and 5 mmol/L
Lactate between 3 and 4 mmol/L
correctOption: Lactate <2 mmol/L
optionExplanations: Correct. A lactate level below 2 mmol/L is the classic physiological index used to suggest a patient is adequately resuscitated and suitable for Early Total Care.
A lactate of 2.5 with an upward trend is concerning and suggests the patient is not yet stable enough for ETC.
A lactate >5 mmol/L is a strong indication for Damage Control Surgery (DCS), not Early Total Care.
This range indicates significant under-resuscitation, necessitating further resuscitation or DCS.
Lactate >3 mmol/L indicates the patient is under-resuscitated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): Venous lactate is an essential marker of resuscitation... <2 mmol/L – ETC; 2–3 mmol/L – look at the trend... >3 mmol/L – may be under-resuscitated; should either have further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent; >5 mmol/L – DCS.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In the management of an open pneumothorax ('sucking chest wound'), what is the correct technique for applying a dressing to prevent the development of a tension pneumothorax?
options: Applying a completely occlusive airtight dressing taped on all four sides
Immediate primary surgical closure of the chest wall defect
Applying a porous dressing to allow continuous air equilibration
Applying a sterile occlusive plastic dressing taped on only three sides
Placing a thick gauze pack directly into the wound secured with a firm bandage
correctOption: Applying a sterile occlusive plastic dressing taped on only three sides
optionExplanations: Taping all four sides can trap air in the pleural space, converting an open pneumothorax into a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.
Primary surgical closure should never be attempted until a chest drain is in place to avoid creating a tension pneumothorax.
A porous dressing would allow air to continue entering the pleural space, failing to resolve the hypoventilation associated with the open defect.
Correct. Taping on three sides creates a flutter valve that allows air to escape during expiration but prevents it from being sucked in during inspiration.
Packs do not provide a controlled valve effect and can fail to stop air entry or conversely trap air inside.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): Initial management consists of promptly closing the defect with a sterile occlusive plastic dressing... taped on three sides to act as a futter-type valve. A chest tube is inserted as soon as possible in a site remote from the injury site.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: An 82-year-old female presents after a fall with suspected pelvic instability. While awaiting radiographic confirmation, which of the following is the correct acute management plan regarding a pelvic binder and patient movement?
options: Apply the binder at the level of the greater trochanters and avoid any rolling beyond 20 degrees
Wait for CT confirmation before applying the binder to avoid skin pressure ulcers
Apply the binder at the level of the iliac crests and log-roll the patient 90 degrees to check for back injuries
Remove the binder as soon as possible to allow for clinical examination of the perineum
Perform 'springing of the pelvis' to confirm the fracture before binder application
correctOption: Apply the binder at the level of the greater trochanters and avoid any rolling beyond 20 degrees
optionExplanations: Correct. The binder must be placed at the greater trochanters to effectively reduce pelvic volume. Movement should be limited to a 20-degree roll (using a scoop stretcher if available) until fracture is ruled out.
The binder is a life-saving resuscitation tool and must be applied in the ED based on clinical suspicion/instability, not delayed for CT.
The binder must be at the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests. 90-degree log-rolling is contraindicated as it can disrupt blood clots in a pelvic fracture.
The binder should not be removed until a pelvic fracture has been radiographically excluded.
Springing the pelvis is strictly contraindicated as it provides no useful info and can cause massive re-bleeding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 357 (Book Page): Log-rolling patients with severe pelvic fractures may harm the patient by disturbing established blood clots... if patients need to be moved... a 20° roll with inline spinal stabilisation should be used. Page 356 (Book Page): A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy. Page 358 (Book Page): Mechanical testing of the pelvis... should never be performed.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A hospital receives a 'Code Red' trauma call for a patient with massive torso haemorrhage. According to established massive transfusion protocols (MTP), what is the recommended ratio of blood products for resuscitation?
options: 1 Packed cells : 2 Fresh-frozen plasma : 4 Platelets
1 Packed cells : 1 Fresh-frozen plasma : 1 Platelets
4 Packed cells : 1 Fresh-frozen plasma : 0 Platelets
5 Packed cells : 5 Crystalloid units : 1 Platelet pack
2 Packed cells : 1 Fresh-frozen plasma : 1 Albumin
correctOption: 1 Packed cells : 1 Fresh-frozen plasma : 1 Platelets
optionExplanations: This ratio provides excessive plasma and platelets relative to oxygen-carrying packed cells.
Correct. Modern damage control resuscitation utilizes a balanced 1:1:1 ratio to mimic whole blood and prevent trauma-induced coagulopathy.
This ratio lacks platelets and has insufficient FFP, increasing the risk of dilutional coagulopathy.
Excessive crystalloids should be avoided in severe haemorrhage as they cause haemodilution and worsen the lethal triad.
Albumin is a colloid and is not part of the standard 1:1:1 MTP for acute haemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A patient with a zygomatic complex fracture develops a tense proptosis, reduced visual acuity, and an afferent pupillary defect. What is the definitive immediate management for this potential complication?
options: Application of ice packs and urgent ophthalmology referral for the next day
Manual reduction of the zygomatic bone under local anaesthesia
Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis
Administration of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids
Performing an emergency CT scan to locate the haematoma
correctOption: Immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis
optionExplanations: This is a surgical emergency; delaying for a referral or using ice packs will result in permanent blindness.
Bone reduction does not address the soft-tissue compartment pressure causing the optic nerve ischaemia.
Correct. Lateral canthotomy and cantholysis is a sight-saving emergency procedure to decompress the orbit when retrobulbar haemorrhage is suspected.
Steroids are an adjunct but do not provide the necessary immediate surgical decompression to save sight.
Diagnosis is clinical. One should not delay for a CT scan if the clinical signs of orbital compartment syndrome (retrobulbar haemorrhage) are present.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): A retrobulbar haemorrhage is an acute surgical emergency as it can lead to blindness... It presents with tense proptosis, increasing pain, reduced visual acuity and loss of the pupillary response... If this is suspected, preparation should be made for immediate bedside lateral canthotomy and cantholysis under LA.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In the initial management of a severely injured trauma patient without a suspected head injury, what is the recommended target systolic blood pressure to be maintained during the time-limited period of permissive hypotension?
options: 90–110 mmHg
Over 120 mmHg
50–70 mmHg
70–90 mmHg
correctOption: 70–90 mmHg
optionExplanations: 90–110 mmHg is the specific target if a head injury is suspected to ensure cerebral perfusion, but higher than necessary for isolated torso trauma.
Normal or high BP is actively avoided in the initial resuscitation phase before surgical hemorrhage control.
50-70 mmHg is too low and risks critical hypoperfusion to the heart and kidneys even for short durations.
110–120 mmHg exceeds the targets of permissive hypotension and can dislodge newly formed clots (clot blowout).
70–90 mmHg is the target range for permissive hypotension in trauma to maintain vital organ perfusion while minimizing the exacerbation of internal hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A 24-year-old male sustains blunt torso trauma. During resuscitation, the clinical team is cautioned against excessive intravenous crystalloid use. What specific pathophysiological cascade is primarily triggered by over-administration of these fluids in this context?
options: Hypernatraemia and intracellular dehydration
Activation of the fibrinolytic pathway via plasminogen
Vasoconstriction of peripheral vascular beds leading to lactic acidosis
Haemodilution leading to worsened coagulopathy and adult respiratory distress syndrome
Acute kidney injury due to decreased renal blood flow
correctOption: Haemodilution leading to worsened coagulopathy and adult respiratory distress syndrome
optionExplanations: Crystalloids like normal saline typically cause hyponatremia or hyperchloremic acidosis rather than hypernatraemic intracellular dehydration.
While hemorrhage activates fibrinolysis, crystalloids do not directly activate plasminogen; they dilute clotting factors.
Crystalloids are volume expanders and would technically reduce reflex vasoconstriction, not cause it, though they may worsen acidosis through other pathways.

Large volumes of crystalloid dilute the concentration of clotting factors and platelets (haemodilution), worsening trauma-induced coagulopathy and increasing pulmonary interstitial fluid, which leads to ARDS.
Excessive crystalloids initially increase renal perfusion but can lead to renal edema, not primary AKI via reduced flow.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: When utilizing the clinical predictors established by Kocher et al. to differentiate between septic arthritis and transient synovitis in a limping child, which combination of findings yields a 93% probability of the joint being septic?
options: Age <4 years, history of trauma, and ESR >40 mm/h
History of fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing, and ESR >20 mm/h
Fever >38.5°C, ESR >40 mm/h, white cell count >12 × 10⁹/L, and non-weight-bearing
Bilateral involvement, fever >38.5°C, and WCC >12 × 10⁹/L
WCC >12 × 10⁹/L, CRP >20 mg/L, and non-weight-bearing
correctOption: Fever >38.5°C, ESR >40 mm/h, white cell count >12 × 10⁹/L, and non-weight-bearing
optionExplanations: Age and trauma history are common factors but are not part of the predictive scoring system used to differentiate these two specific conditions.
ESR must be >40 mm/h per Kocher's study to be one of the four key predictors.
Meeting all four specific criteria (Fever, Non-weight-bearing, ESR >40, WCC >12) correlates to a 93% probability of septic arthritis.
Septic arthritis is almost always monoarticular; bilateral involvement would typically point away from simple septic arthritis.
While CRP is often used clinically, it was not one of the four primary variables in the original 93% probability model by Kocher.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): (a) The clinical predictors of Kocher et al. (2004) for the diagnosis of septic arthritis: ● History of fever >38.5°C ● Non-weight-bearing ● Erythrocyte sedimentation rate >40 mm/h ● White cell count >12 × 10 9 /L... Number of positive predictors: 4 - Predicted probability of joint sepsis: 93.0%

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
coreConcept: Identifying Indications for Damage Control Surgery
statement: A 35-year-old polytrauma patient is in the operating room. Intraoperatively, the patient's temperature is 33.5°C, pH is 7.15, and the serum lactate is measured at 6.0 mmol/L. According to the principles of Damage Control Surgery (DCS), what is the immediate plan for management?
options: Perform a complete primary, secondary, and tertiary survey while the abdomen remains open
Continue the procedure only until all anatomical repairs of bowel and liver are perfect
Administer 10 units of crystalloid to normalize the lactate before closing the wound
Proceed with definitive Early Total Care (ETC) and internal fixation of all long bone fractures
Perform only rapid life-saving procedures (hemorrhage and contamination control) and move the patient to ICU for physiological stabilization
correctOption: Perform only rapid life-saving procedures (hemorrhage and contamination control) and move the patient to ICU for physiological stabilization
optionExplanations: The tertiary survey is deferred until the patient is extubated and alert; the primary focus now is abbreviated surgical intervention.
Lengthy complex reconstructions or perfect anatomical repairs consume time and worsen the physiological status in DCS-indicated patients.
Lactate is a marker of perfusion, but excessive crystalloids cause haemodilution and worsen coagulopathy; blood products are preferred.
ETC is contraindicated here because the patient has the 'triad of death' (hypothermia <34°C, acidosis pH <7.2, and lactate >5 mmol/L).
The patient meets all criteria for DCS: lactate >5, pH <7.2, and temp <34°C. The goal is to stop bleeding/contamination and get to the ICU to correct the physiology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): The ‘triad of death’ – a cycle of acidosis, coagulopathy and hypothermia – may develop and result in multiorgan failure and death. Consequently, surgical interventions in the trauma patient with physiological abnormality are limited to rapid life- and limb-saving procedures: control of haemorrhage, decompression of cavities... revascularisation of ischaemic organs and limbs and removal of contamination. This damage control approach aims to rapidly achieve these objectives and then move the patient to a critical care environment and continue with resuscitation.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A patient arrives at the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident with a pulse of 115 bpm and systolic blood pressure of 105 mmHg. What is the correct immediate pharmacological administration protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA) according to the provided standards?
options: 1g given intramuscularly to prevent rapid absorption and potential hypotension
1g given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1g dose over 8 hours
500mg given intravenously every 4 hours for the first 24 hours
2g as a single slow intravenous bolus over 30 minutes
1g given as a continuous infusion over 24 hours only
correctOption: 1g given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1g dose over 8 hours
optionExplanations: TXA in acute trauma is given intravenously for immediate systemic effect; IM absorption is too slow and unreliable for exsanguinating hemorrhage.
The loading dose of 1g over 10 mins followed by 1g over 8 hours is the standard established by clinical trials (CRASH-2) mentioned in the text.
The protocol is strictly a two-stage administration (bolus then 8-hour infusion), not a multi-dose every 4 hours.
Standard protocol involves a loading dose and then a maintenance infusion, not a 2g single bolus.
Only using a slow infusion without a loading dose would delay the therapeutic concentration needed to stabilize early clots.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute... One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In the clinical classification of head injury severity, which component of the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is statistically recognized as the best predictor of neurological outcome?
options: Motor score
Respiratory rate and pattern
Verbal response
Pupillary light reflex
Eye opening response
correctOption: Motor score
optionExplanations: The motor score is the most reliable predictor of overall neurological outcome in traumatic brain injury according to neurosurgical guidelines.
Respiratory patterns (like in Cushing’s triad) are signs of brainstem compromise but are not components of the GCS classification system.
Verbal response can be complicated by intubation or drugs and is not as strong a prognostic indicator as the motor component.
Pupillary reflex is a clinical sign of herniation/pressure but is not a component of the GCS score itself.
Eye opening reflects arousal but is less predictive of final functional outcome than the motor score.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 361 (Book Page): The severity of head injury is classifed according to the post-resuscitation Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score (Table 28.1), as it is the GCS score – and in particular the motor score – that is the best predictor of neurological outcome.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A patient with suspected blunt pelvic trauma is hemodynamically unstable. According to trauma management principles, which action is most critical regarding the use of a pelvic binder?
options: It must be loosened every 30 minutes to prevent skin necrosis from pressure
The binder should be positioned at the level of the greater trochanters and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded
It should be applied at the level of the umbilicus for optimal compression
It should be removed immediately before any trauma laparotomy to allow access to the abdomen
The pelvis should be mechanically 'sprung' to confirm the fracture before application
correctOption: The binder should be positioned at the level of the greater trochanters and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded
optionExplanations: Loosening the binder in an unstable patient can lead to immediate cardiovascular collapse due to loss of tamponade effect on pelvic venous plexuses.
Proper positioning is over the greater trochanters. It must remain in place to prevent the 'open book' from re-expanding and causing fatal venous bleeding.
Placing it at the umbilicus is incorrect; it must be over the greater trochanters to reduce the pelvic volume and stabilize the ring.
The text explicitly states a correctly positioned binder does not obstruct laparotomy and should not be removed.
'Springing' the pelvis is dangerous as it can disrupt stable clots and worsen hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded... A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: A 40-year-old female presents following severe traumatic brain injury. After initial stabilization, she develops polyuria with very dilute urine and rising serum sodium (>150 mmol/L). What is the most likely cause of this complication in the context of her injury?
options: Cerebral Salt Wasting (CSW)
Psychogenic polydipsia
Diabetes Insipidus
Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone (SIADH)
Acute Tubular Necrosis (ATN)
correctOption: Diabetes Insipidus
optionExplanations: Cerebral Salt Wasting leads to volume depletion and hyponatraemia.
Psychogenic polydipsia involves excessive water intake, which would typically cause low sodium, and is unrelated to the pathophysiology of traumatic pituitary insult.
Diabetes Insipidus occurs when trauma disrupts ADH secretion, leading to the inability to concentrate urine, excessive free water loss, and consequent hypernatraemia.
SIADH causes water retention and hyponatraemia, not hypernatraemia.
ATN usually presents with oliguria (low urine output) and rising potassium/creatinine rather than massive polyuria and high sodium.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 369 (Book Page): Conversely antidiuretic hormone secretion may be compromised in the context of trauma, producing diabetes insipidus, resulting in hypernatraemia.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: Which set of findings constitutes 'Cushing's Triad', a physiological loop indicating imminent brainstem herniation due to raised intracranial pressure?
options: Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy
Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration
Hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnoea
Hypertension, tachycardia, and dilated pupils
Hypotension, bradycardia, and mufed heart sounds
correctOption: Hypertension, bradycardia, and irregular respiration
optionExplanations: This is the 'Triad of Death' for surgical hemorrhage, not Cushing's triad.
Hypertension (compensatory to maintain CPP), bradycardia (reflex), and irregular breathing (brainstem compression) characterize this late, ominous sign.
This is the classic triad of hypovolaemic shock, the opposite of the Cushing response.
Tachycardia is not part of the triad, although dilated pupils often accompany herniation syndromes.
Muffled heart sounds and hypotension with bradycardia point toward cardiac tamponade or neurogenic shock, not raised ICP.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 361 (Book Page): Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing’s triad: hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.

category: Outline plan for acute management and identify potential complications
statement: In a hospital's massive transfusion protocol for severely injured patients with hypovolaemic shock, what is the standard recommended ratio for the administration of blood and blood products?
options: 2 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets
1 packed red cells : 2 fresh-frozen plasma : 0 platelets
3 packed red cells : 3 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets
4 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets
1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets
correctOption: 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets
optionExplanations: This ratio is sometimes used in non-trauma settings but current trauma guidance insists on a balanced 1:1:1 ratio.
Omitting platelets entirely would fail to manage trauma-induced coagulopathy.
While the FFP:RBC ratio is correct here, the overall standard is expressed in the simplest 1:1:1 terms.
This older 'high-red-cell' ratio is associated with increased coagulopathy in trauma patients.
The 1:1:1 ratio is designed to mimic whole blood and prevent the dilution of clotting factors and platelets.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): All hospitals managing severe trauma should have a massive transfusion protocol that aims to provide blood and blood products in a ratio of 1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
statement: Which clinical observation is considered a diagnostic sign for increased forefoot abduction and a splayed forefoot in a patient with a suspected pes planus deformity?
options: The ‘J-sign’ during active knee extension
The presence of a dinner fork deformity
A positive Stener lesion on thumb stress
A positive Trendelenburg sign on standing
The ‘too many toes’ sign seen from behind
correctOption: The ‘too many toes’ sign seen from behind
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The J-sign relates to patellar maltracking as the knee moves into full extension.
Incorrect. The dinner fork deformity is characteristic of a Colles' fracture of the distal radius, not a foot deformity.
Incorrect. A Stener lesion refers to a specific ligamentous injury in the thumb where the adductor aponeurosis is interposed between the ruptured ulnar collateral ligament and its insertion.
Incorrect. The Trendelenburg sign is used to assess the strength of the hip abductors, not the architecture of the foot.
Correct. The 'too many toes' sign is a classic clinical finding in flat feet, where the heel valgus and forefoot abduction make more toes visible from a posterior view than in a neutral foot.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 473 (Book Page): The ‘too many toes’ sign demonstrates increased forefoot abduction (pes planus [fat foot]) and a splayed forefoot.

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
coreConcept: Mechanical Strain and Tissue Differentiation in Bone Healing
statement: In accordance with Perren’s theory of bone healing, how does the magnitude of interfragmentary strain influence the final tissue differentiation at a fracture site?
options: Strain at 0% is required to initiate indirect secondary bone healing
Strain under 2% promotes hard callus and mineralisation
Strain under 100% results in immediate mature lamellar bone
Strain between 10% and 100% promotes primary osteonal healing
Any level of strain over 2% inhibits callus formation entirely
correctOption: Strain under 2% promotes hard callus and mineralisation
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Indirect healing requires some relative movement (strain); absolute 0% strain would promote direct bone healing instead.
Correct. According to Perren, a low-strain environment (less than 2%) allows for the formation of hard callus and subsequent mineralisation, leading to stable union.
Incorrect. Strain under 100% but at high levels leads to the formation of fibrous tissue, not mature bone.
Incorrect. Primary osteonal (direct) healing requires absolute stability and cortical apposition, which is effectively 0% strain.
Incorrect. Strain levels above 2% (up to 10%) actually promote the formation of soft callus, which is an integral part of indirect healing.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 403 (Book Page): The amount of strain determines the nature of tissue it diferentiates into: under 100% leads to fbrous tissue, under 10% soft callus, less than 2% hard callus and progressive mineralisation (Perren’s theory of bone healing).

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Septic Joint vs. Osteomyelitis Sympathetic Effusion
statement: How should a sterile joint aspirate, characterized by the absence of bacteria on microscopy, be interpreted in a child presenting with a hot joint and adjacent metaphyseal tenderness?
options: It definitively confirms the diagnosis of transient synovitis
It should raise suspicion of a sympathetic effusion from metaphyseal osteomyelitis
It mandates the immediate discontinuation of all antimicrobial investigations
It excludes the possibility of bone involvement in the affected limb
It identifies the condition as a non-inflammatory ligamentous injury
correctOption: It should raise suspicion of a sympathetic effusion from metaphyseal osteomyelitis
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While transient synovitis presents with sterile effusions, the presence of metaphyseal tenderness strongly suggests osteomyelitis, which must be ruled out.

Correct. Metaphyseal osteomyelitis can cause a reactionary 'sympathetic' effusion in the neighboring joint. If the aspirate is clear but clinical signs of bone infection persist, the underlying bone must be investigated.
Incorrect. Absence of organisms on initial microscopy does not exclude infection; cultures and further imaging (like MRI) are necessary.
Incorrect. It actually increases the suspicion of underlying bone (metaphyseal) involvement rather than primary joint involvement.
Incorrect. A hot, swollen joint with fever and high markers is unlikely to be a simple ligamentous injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 614 (Book Page): The diferentiation between the two may be difcult and a sympathetic joint efusion may occur with metaphyseal osteomyelitis. Thus, if there are no organisms seen on microscopy of a joint aspirate, the possibility of a coexisting osteomyelitis must be considered.

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
coreConcept: Kocher's Clinical Prediction Rules for Pediatric Septic Arthritis
statement: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic unable to bear weight on the right leg. The child has a fever of 39°C. Laboratory results show a white cell count of 14 × 10^9/L and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 48 mm/h. Radiographs of the hip are normal. What is the calculated probability of septic arthritis in this patient based on Kocher’s clinical predictors?
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This probability (2.0%) corresponds to zero positive predictors.

Correct. This patient meets all four of Kocher's criteria: fever >38.5°C, non-weight-bearing status, ESR >40 mm/h, and WCC >12 × 10^9/L. According to the validated table, four positive predictors correlate with a 93% probability of septic arthritis.
Incorrect. This probability (35.0%) corresponds to exactly two positive predictors.
Incorrect. This probability (9.5%) corresponds to exactly one positive predictor.
Incorrect. This probability (72.8%) corresponds to exactly three positive predictors.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 613 (Book Page): Table 44.17 (b) ... Number of positive predictors ... 4 ... Predicted probability of joint sepsis ... 93.0%

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
coreConcept: Microbiological Yield Optimization in Chronic Osteomyelitis
statement: What is the recommended pharmacological strategy regarding antibiotics for a systemically stable patient prior to an elective surgical biopsy for chronic osteomyelitis?
options: Intense triple-therapy is required immediately to prevent sequestrum formation
Suppressive oral therapy should be continued up until the morning of surgery
Empiric intravenous therapy must be started 48 hours before the procedure
Antibiotics should be stopped for at least 2 weeks before the procedure
A single dose of vancomycin should be given at the time of clinical diagnosis
correctOption: Antibiotics should be stopped for at least 2 weeks before the procedure
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Sequestrum formation is a feature of established chronic disease; immediate antibiotics without a culture are counter-productive in the elective setting.
Incorrect. Continuing suppressive therapy masks the infection and prevents the laboratory from identifying the causative organism.
Incorrect. Giving empiric antibiotics before biopsy can lead to 'culture-negative' results, making definitive targeted therapy impossible.
Correct. To ensure the highest diagnostic yield from bone biopsies, any existing antimicrobial therapy should be paused for 2 weeks to allow for effective pathogen recovery in cultures.
Incorrect. A single dose given early significantly reduces the sensitivity of surgical cultures without treating the chronic underlying disease.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 578 (Book Page): In most cases, it is safe to delay antibiotics until defnitive operative microbiological samples have been taken... if safe to do so, antibiotics should be stopped at least 2 weeks before biopsy or surgery.

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
statement: Which clinical presentation is characteristic of a pediatric 'white eye' blowout fracture of the orbital floor?
options: Immediate loss of red color perception in the affected eye
Profuse bleeding from the ear and periorbital ecchymosis
Inability to look upward without subconjunctival haemorrhage
Severe proptosis accompanied by a fixed and dilated pupil
A palpable step deformity on the supraorbital ridge
correctOption: Inability to look upward without subconjunctival haemorrhage
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Loss of red color perception is an early sign of optic nerve compression (retrobulbar haemorrhage), not simple muscle entrapment.
Incorrect. Periorbital ecchymosis (raccoon eyes) and ear bleeding suggest a base of skull fracture.

Correct. Pediatric orbital fractures can occur as 'trapdoor' events where the bone buckles, traps the inferior rectus muscle, and snaps back, often without showing the external bleeding (subconjunctival haemorrhage) typical of adult fractures.
Incorrect. These are signs of a retrobulbar haemorrhage, a surgical emergency distinct from a 'white eye' blowout.
Incorrect. Supraorbital ridge steps indicate a roof of the orbit or frontal bone fracture.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 392 (Book Page): They are also described as a ‘white eye’ blowout fracture as children often present with no subconjunctival haemorrhage (Figure 31.15).

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
coreConcept: Radiographic Criteria for Cervical Spine Instability
statement: When assessing for cervical spine instability on a lateral radiograph, what is the specific threshold for sagittal angulation considered diagnostic of an unstable segment?
options: Any degree of angulation if the spinolaminar line is intact
Greater than 20 degrees irrespective of adjacent levels
Greater than 3.5 degrees relative to the adjacent level
Exactly 5 degrees with associated soft tissue swelling
Greater than 11 degrees relative to the adjacent level
correctOption: Greater than 11 degrees relative to the adjacent level
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The spinolaminar line is used for alignment, but its integrity does not negate a measurement of significant angulation elsewhere.
Incorrect. The threshold is 11 degrees, and it is assessed specifically against the adjacent level to determine segmental failure.
Incorrect. 3.5 mm is the measurement used for translation, not degrees for angulation.
Incorrect. 5 degrees is below the threshold for defining traumatic instability.
Correct. A difference in angulation between two adjacent vertebral bodies of more than 11 degrees is a recognized radiographic criterion for mechanical instability in the cervical spine.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 371 (Book Page): Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
statement: A 30-year-old trauma victim is brought to the emergency department with a suspected spinal cord injury at the level of T2. Vitals show a BP of 80/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 52 bpm. The skin is warm and dry. What is the pathophysiological explanation for this circulatory state?
options: Myocardial stunning from a blunt cardiac contusion
Unopposed vagal tone from loss of sympathetic outflow
Temporary physiological disorganisation lasting 6 weeks
Massive systemic release of endotoxins and cytokines
Intravascular volume depletion from occult hemorrhage
correctOption: Unopposed vagal tone from loss of sympathetic outflow
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Cardiogenic shock might cause hypotension and bradycardia, but it typically presents with signs of cardiac failure rather than warm peripheries.

Correct. Neurogenic shock occurs when a spinal cord injury above T5 interrupts sympathetic fibers. The resulting unopposed parasympathetic (vagal) tone causes bradycardia and peripheral vasodilation (warm/dry skin), distinguishing it from hypovolemic shock.
Incorrect. This describes 'Spinal Shock,' which is a neurological phenomenon of loss of reflexes, not a hemodynamic (circulatory) syndrome.
Incorrect. This describes septic shock, which would typically present with a fever and a likely focus of infection, not acute trauma-induced warm hypotension/bradycardia.
Incorrect. Hypovolemic shock presents with tachycardia (compensatory) and cold, clammy skin due to peripheral vasoconstriction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outfow (T5).

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
statement: Which developmental principle describes the mechanism where tensile forces stimulate skeletal growth while compressive forces inhibit it?
options: Gächter staging system
Salter–Harris classification
Monro–Kellie doctrine
Wolff’s law
Hueter–Volkmann principle
correctOption: Hueter–Volkmann principle
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Gächter staging is used to grade the severity of synovial involvement in septic arthritis.
Incorrect. Salter-Harris is a classification for types of growth plate fractures, not a physiological growth law.
Incorrect. The Monro-Kellie doctrine relates to intracranial pressure and the volume of contents within the rigid skull.

Incorrect. Wolff’s law describes how bone remodels its internal structure (deposition and resorption) based on applied loads, but it is not specific to the inhibition/stimulation of longitudinal growth centers.

Correct. The Hueter-Volkmann principle explains how asymmetrical pressures on a growth plate can cause or correct deformities; it is the basis for using braces or guided growth in pediatric orthopaedics.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 588 (Book Page): Table 44.1 Hueter–Volkmann principle: Compressive forces inhibit growth; Tensile forces stimulate growth.

category: Interpret relevant clinical and radiological findings used in diagnosing skeletal involvement
statement: Which clinical presentation is most characteristic of a late-onset, indolent prosthetic joint infection (PJI)?
options: 'Start-up' symptoms of joint discomfort
High-grade fever and a rapidly spreading cellulitis
A dinner fork deformity at the site of the prosthesis
Acute septic shock with multi-organ failure
A tense, painful joint with immediate loss of pulses
correctOption: 'Start-up' symptoms of joint discomfort
optionExplanations: Correct. Indolent PJIs, often caused by low-virulence organisms like coagulase-negative staphylococci, typically present with mechanical-style pain, particularly pain when first starting to move (start-up pain).
Incorrect. These are features of early PJI or acute haematogenous spread, not the slow, 'indolent' late-onset version.
Incorrect. Dinner fork deformity is a radiographic/clinical appearance of a Colles' fracture, not an implant infection sign.
Incorrect. This describes a fulminant acute infection, not an indolent late presentation.
Incorrect. Loss of pulses suggests vascular injury or compartment syndrome, not chronic implant infection.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 579 (Book Page): Late infections are more likely to present with an indolent clinical syndrome of joint discomfort or mechanical dysfunction (‘start-up’ symptoms are particularly characteristic), with or without a discharging sinus.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
coreConcept: Gold Standard for Major Trauma Imaging
statement: In the initial assessment of a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient, which of the following imaging protocols is considered the gold standard for identifying life-threatening internal pathologies?
options: Immediate routine whole-body CT (WBCT) based solely on high-energy mechanism of injury
Selective CT scanning restricted to the primary zone of injury identified on clinical examination
Triple-phase bone scintigraphy to evaluate for occult fractures not seen on primary surveys
Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast for patients with deranged physiology
Sequential plain radiography of the chest and pelvis followed by ultrasonography of the abdomen
correctOption: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast for patients with deranged physiology
optionExplanations: The source material notes that WBCT should not be performed on the basis of mechanism of injury alone, but rather based on signs, symptoms, or deranged physiology.
Selective scanning is specifically stated to have no role in the severely injured trauma patient; a comprehensive approach is required to catch occult multiple sources of hemorrhage.
Nuclear medicine scans like scintigraphy are not used in the acute trauma primary survey as they lack the speed and anatomical detail required for immediate life-saving decisions.
WBCT with IV contrast covering the head to pelvis is the diagnostic benchmark for polytrauma patients showing signs of physiological derangement.
While traditional, these plain films are increasingly omitted in favor of rapid CT scans when the patient is hemodynamically unstable or in significant trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A trauma patient in the supine position requires a chest radiograph to evaluate for thoracic injury. Which pathophysiological principle explains why a supine radiograph may yield an confusing image of a haemothorax?
options: Supine positioning causes a 'shroud effect' where the heart shadow obscures any blood in the costophrenic angles
Blood pools anteriorly in the pleural space, mimicking a pneumothorax due to increased radiolucency
The infated lung 'foats' on the haemothorax, causing a homogeneous increase in opacity across the hemithorax
Blood pools behind the domes of the diaphragm, making up to 1000 mL completely invisible
Gravity-dependent blood collection causes the trachea to deviate toward the side of the haemothorax
correctOption: The infated lung 'foats' on the haemothorax, causing a homogeneous increase in opacity across the hemithorax
optionExplanations: The heart shadow is an anatomical constant; the confusion arises from the global layering of blood posteriorly across the entire lung field, not specific concealment by the mediastinum.
Blood pools posteriorly in a supine patient due to gravity, leading to increased opacity (whiteness), not radiolucency.

In a supine radiograph, the blood layers out posteriorly, making the entire hemithorax appear uniformly more opaque. This is confusing because the 'darker' side (the normal side) might be mistaken for a pneumothorax.
Up to 300 mL of blood may pool behind the domes of the diaphragm and be invisible, but the source does not cite 1000 mL for this specific hidden volume.
Tracheal deviation is characteristic of tension pneumothorax (away from injury) or lung collapse (toward injury), not simple supine haemothorax layering.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 373 (Book Page): a supine chest radiograph can show a haemothorax as a homogeneous increase in opacity of the hemithorax – this can cause confusion between the darker side and the lighter side as to which may be a haemothorax (less radiolucent) or a pneumothorax (more radiolucent); look carefully for lung markings and do not drain the wrong side

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A 72-year-old patient presents with insidious neurological deterioration and a history of a trivial fall three weeks ago. On CT imaging, how does the radiological density of a chronic subdural haematoma typically differ from that of an acute extradural haematoma?
options: Chronic subdural haematomas are concave hyperdense lesions, while extradural haematomas are diffuse and isodense
Chronic subdural haematomas are constrained by dural adherence to the skull, while extradural lesions are free to expand across the surface
Chronic subdural haematomas appear lentiform and hyperdense, while extradural lesions are concave and hypodense
Chronic subdural haematomas show 'swirl signs' of active bleeding, while extradural haematomas demonstrate osmotic expansion
Chronic subdural haematomas appear as diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface, whereas extradural haematomas are typically hyperdense lentiform lesions
correctOption: Chronic subdural haematomas appear as diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface, whereas extradural haematomas are typically hyperdense lentiform lesions
optionExplanations: Diffuse isodensity can occur in subdural haematomas of intermediate age, but the standard chronic presentation is hypodense. Extradural lesions are almost always biconvex/lentiform, not diffuse.
This is anatomically reversed; the dura is adherent to the skull (extradural restricted), but not adherent to the brain (subdural free to spread).
Extradural haematomas are lentiform and hyperdense, while subdural haematomas are concave. Chronic subdurals are hypodense (old blood).
The swirl sign indicates acute active bleeding in an extradural haematoma; chronic subdural haematomas expand via osmosis as the clot degrades.

The breakdown of blood over weeks in a chronic subdural leads to hypodensity. Extradural haematomas are acute, arterial/venous sinus bleeds that are restricted by the dura's adherence to skull sutures, creating the biconvex shape.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 365 (Book Page) and 388: On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion... Imaging [of chronic subdural haematoma] reveals diffuse hypodensity overlying the brain surface.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A patient arrives after a high-speed vehicle collision with a pulse of 125/min, BP 85/50 mmHg, and chest wall contusion. An erect chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. Which clinical and imaging principle applies to this patient's management?
options: Immediate surgical repair of the aorta is mandatory based solely on the erect radiograph findings
A lateral decubitus radiograph should be performed next to assess for a fuid meniscus in the mediastinal space
The patient must be transferred immediately for MRI to rule out ligamentous thoracic spine injury
Widening of the mediastinum on radiograph is the definitive cause of the patient's current hypotension
Widening of the mediastinum on radiograph suggests aortic injury, but it is unlikely to be the primary cause of hypotension as complete disruptions rarely reach the hospital
correctOption: Widening of the mediastinum on radiograph suggests aortic injury, but it is unlikely to be the primary cause of hypotension as complete disruptions rarely reach the hospital
optionExplanations: Confirmation by CT of the mediastinum or angiography is required before surgical repair, and the patient's hypotension must be addressed simultaneously.
Lateral decubitus is used to assess pleural effusion, not mediastinal widening or aortic disruption.
MRI is too slow for an unstable trauma patient with BP 85/50; stabilization and CT are the priorities.
The source material explicitly states that aortic injury is NOT the cause of hypotension in those who survive to reach the hospital; other concurrent injuries (like abdominal bleed) are responsible.

Widened mediastinum is the classic CXR sign for aortic rupture, but because complete rupture is usually fatal instantly, the survivors seen in the ED with hypotension likely have other occult bleeding sources.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): In the hypotensive patient, widening of the mediastinum and aortic injury is not the cause of the hypotension. Invariably, these patients have other injuries causing hypotension as patients with complete aortic disruption rarely, if ever, survive to reach hospital.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
coreConcept: NICE Guidelines for Head Injury CT
statement: According to current guidelines, a 70-year-old patient who sustained a head injury from a low-velocity fall but is currently on Warfarin requires a CT scan of the brain within which timeframe?
options: Immediately upon arrival if the GCS is 15 and they have no amnesia
Only if they exhibit focal neurological defcits or persistent vomiting
Within 1 hour of the injury regardless of GCS score
Within 8 hours of the injury as part of the coagulopathy risk assessment
Delayed for 24 hours to allow for potential 'lucid interval' expansion
correctOption: Within 8 hours of the injury as part of the coagulopathy risk assessment
optionExplanations: If GCS is 15 and there is no amnesia, the 1-hour criteria are not met, but the patient still falls into the 8-hour category due to medication and age.
While these are indications for a 1-hour CT, they are not the only criteria; coagulopathy itself mandates imaging in this age group within 8 hours.
CT within 1 hour is reserved for GCS <13, focal neurological deficits, suspected skull fractures, or seizures.
Age over 65 and use of anticoagulants are specific criteria for obtaining a CT scan within an 8-hour window, as the risk of intracranial hemorrhage is higher even with minor mechanisms.
Waiting 24 hours is dangerous in an anticoagulated patient; early imaging is needed to detect bleeds before they cause mass effect.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 362 (Book Page): Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours: Age >65, Coagulopathy (e.g. aspirin, warfarin or rivaroxaban use)

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: When assessing suspected extremity trauma using the 'Rule of 2s' for plain radiography, what specific requirement must be met regarding the chronological evaluation of the injury?
options: Two different imaging modalities (e.g., X-ray and Ultrasound) must be used simultaneously
Two radiographs must be taken 2 hours apart in the acute phase to monitor for swelling
The injury must be imaged twice: once in the emergency department and once post-operatively
Two different radiologists must interpret the flms independently to reduce missed fracture rates
Radiographs should be taken on two occasions (e.g., 10–14 days later) if initial views are normal but symptoms persist
correctOption: Radiographs should be taken on two occasions (e.g., 10–14 days later) if initial views are normal but symptoms persist
optionExplanations: The rule refers to X-rays in two planes (AP/Lateral), two joints (above/below), two occasions (now/later), and two sides (injured/normal).
The 'Rule of 2s' refers to a 10-14 day gap for occult fractures (like scaphoid), not a 2-hour gap for swelling.
While post-op imaging is standard, it is not the definition of the '2 occasions' rule, which targets diagnostic accuracy for occult injuries.
Dual reporting is a quality control measure but is not part of the clinical 'Rule of 2s'.
This is a critical safety rule to catch fractures that only become radiographically visible once bone resorption occurs at the fracture site after nearly two weeks.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 398 (Book Page): 2 occasions – sometimes the fracture may not be initially visible; a second series of radiographs should be undertaken after 10–14 days if suspicion of bony injury persists.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A patient with a suspected 'open book' pelvic fracture is being evaluated. What is a significant diagnostic pitfall when interpreting their plain radiograph?
options: The 'too many toes' sign will create a projection artifact on the pelvic inlet view
The pelvic binder may normalize the radiographic appearance, masking the severity of the fracture
Gas in the bowel prevents the visualization of fractures in the pubic rami on all standard X-rays
Plain radiographs are only accurate if the patient is placed in a prone position for the AP view
Radiographs are unable to distinguish between venous and arterial sources of pelvic bleeding
correctOption: The pelvic binder may normalize the radiographic appearance, masking the severity of the fracture
optionExplanations: The 'too many toes' sign is a clinical finding of pes planus (Page 495), not a radiological artifact in pelvic imaging.
A correctly applied pelvic binder reduces the pelvic volume and closes the 'open book,' which can make the symphysis appear normal on X-ray even if it is unstable.
Bowel gas can obscure detail but does not make visualization impossible; CT is the gold standard if gas or obesity limits plain films.
Trauma patients are never placed in a prone position for pelvic X-rays due to spine and airway risks; AP supine is the standard.

This statement is true but is not a 'pitfall of interpreting the fracture' on radiograph; rather, it's a limitation of the modality. The normalization of anatomy by a binder is a specific interpretive trap.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 364 (Book Page): It is important to note that the vast majority of patients with suspected pelvic fractures may have a pelvic binder in place and hence plain radiograph fndings may be normal.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: In a hemodynamically unstable patient with blunt torso trauma where there is no time for WBCT, which imaging modality is the most expeditious for locating the primary source of major intra-abdominal or pericardial hemorrhage?
options: Standard erect chest radiograph looking for air-fuid levels
Dynamic MRI angiography to assess for aortic intimal faps
Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST)
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) with aspiration of >10 mL of blood
Three-dimensional reconstruction of the pelvic ring via CT
correctOption: Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST)
optionExplanations: An erect CXR is useful but impossible in an unstable, potentially spinal-injured patient; supine CXR is standard but less sensitive for identifying the *source* of bleeding compared to ultrasound.
MRI has no place in the emergency management of a hemodynamically compromised trauma patient.
eFAST is highly accurate for detecting >100 mL of free blood and can be performed simultaneously with resuscitation in the ED or operating room, making it the fastest choice for an unstable patient.
DPL is used in resource-limited settings and is more invasive; eFAST is now the standard for rapid, non-invasive bedside detection of blood.
CT is inappropriate for a grossly unstable patient who requires immediate surgical control.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of haemorrhage. Page 373 (Book Page): Extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) is becoming the most common investigation... looking for a cardiac tamponade or free blood and air in the hemithoraces, and assessment for blood in the abdominal cavity.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient with moderate traumatic brain injury. Which imaging sequence is most sensitive for evaluating Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI) in a patient who fails to improve neurologically despite an unremarkable initial CT scan?
options: Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the carotid and vertebral arteries
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
Positron emission tomography (PET) to measure glucose metabolism in the cortex
Trans-cranial Doppler ultrasound to measure cerebral blood fow
Repeat non-contrast CT brain at 24 hours to look for delayed 'talk and die' pattern
correctOption: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
optionExplanations: CTA is used to look for arterial dissection or vascular injury, not for axonal injury within the brain parenchyma.
MRI can detect subtle hemorrhagic foci and non-hemorrhagic edema in areas like the corpus callosum that are invisible to CT.
PET is used for metabolic research or chronic states, not for the acute diagnostic evaluation of DAI in the trauma setting.
Trans-cranial Doppler monitors ICP and flow velocity but does not visualize structural axonal damage.
Non-contrast CT is poor at identifying the microscopic shearing of axons characteristic of DAI.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 368 (Book Page): Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: When performing plain radiography for a patient with a gunshot wound to the torso, what is the primary purpose of placing metal markers on all external skin wounds?
options: To provide a reference scale for measuring the exact caliber of the retained bullet
To allow assessment of the trajectory and correlate the number of skin holes with the number of missiles seen internally
To distinguish between an entry wound and an exit wound based on marker orientation
To prevent the 'swirl sign' Projection artifact caused by the metallic projectile
To shield the surrounding tissues from secondary scatter radiation from the bullet
correctOption: To allow assessment of the trajectory and correlate the number of skin holes with the number of missiles seen internally
optionExplanations: Markers (like paper clips) are not calibrated for precise ballistics; they are for anatomical tracking.
This is crucial for identifying 'missing' bullets or identifying if a single projectile caused multiple wounds by passing through different body parts.
Entry and exit wounds are determined by physical examination (soot, tattooing, size); markers just identify that a hole exists for the X-ray ray to 'see'.
The 'swirl sign' is a CT finding of active bleeding (Page 386), not a radiographic artifact related to metal markers.
A paper clip provides zero radiation shielding.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 378 (Book Page): In patients with penetrating injury, metal markers (e.g. bent paper clips) should be placed on all external wounds before plain flms are taken... as this allows an assessment of the trajectory and helps to correlate the number of holes and the number of missiles that can be seen within the patient.

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: In the initial management of an adult blunt trauma patient with multiple injuries and deranged physiology, which imaging modality is currently established as the 'gold standard' investigation?
options: Routine serial plain radiographs of the chest, pelvis, and long bones
Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast
Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST) as the definitive study
Selective computed tomography of the suspected injured system
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the torso and cranium
correctOption: Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast
optionExplanations: Traditional radiographs are increasingly omitted in favor of rapid WBCT, although they may still be used if a patient is too unstable for the CT scanner.
WBCT from head to pelvis with intravenous contrast is the gold standard for major trauma as it rapidly identifies multi-system injuries and directs definitive care.
FAST is a valuable screening tool for free fluid but is not definitive as it cannot accurately identify specific solid organ injuries or retroperitoneal bleeds.
Selective scanning of individual body systems is no longer the standard of care for severely injured polytrauma patients as it may miss occult injuries in other regions.
MRI is not used in the acute resuscitation phase of severe trauma due to long acquisition times and incompatibility with resuscitation equipment.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology

category: Discuss the role of imaging in diagnosis and follow- up
statement: A high-velocity vehicle collision victim presents with a widened mediastinum on an erect supine chest radiograph. Based on the pathophysiology of torso trauma, what is the most likely diagnosis requiring immediate confirmatory imaging?
options: Tension pneumothorax with mediastinal shift
Traumatic aortic disruption
Massive hemothorax with lung collapse
Tracheobronchial injury with subcutaneous emphysema
Esophageal rupture following barotrauma
correctOption: Traumatic aortic disruption
optionExplanations: Tension pneumothorax typically causes tracheal deviation and lung collapse, but not specifically the uniform widening of the superior mediastinum seen in vascular injuries.
Traumatic aortic rupture occurs due to shear forces at the ligamentum arteriosum; the resulting hematoma causes the classic 'widened mediastinum' appearance on imaging.
Massive hemothorax shows as a homogeneous increase in opacity across the hemithorax rather than isolated mediastinal widening.
