category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
coreConcept: Chance Fractures and Associated Visceral Trauma
statement: A 19-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after a high-velocity car collision. She was a rear-seat passenger wearing a lap-only seatbelt. Physical examination reveals transverse bruising across the lower abdomen and acute point tenderness at the T12-L1 junction. Radiographs show a horizontal distraction injury through the posterior elements and vertebral body. Which associated clinical feature is most critical to exclude in this specific injury pattern?
options: Visceral injuries such as duodenal or aortic rupture
Associated calcaneal fracture
Bilateral dislocation of the shoulder
Rupture of the Achilles tendon
Isolated injury to the C1 transverse ligament
correctOption: Visceral injuries such as duodenal or aortic rupture
optionExplanations: Chance fractures result from the body pivoting around a lap belt, causing high-tension forces that frequently rupture hollow viscera (duodenum/pancreas) or the aorta along with the spine.
While calcaneal fractures are associated with axial loading (falls from height), Chance fractures are distraction injuries from seatbelts.
Shoulder dislocations are common in RTA but are not the specific, life-threatening associated clinical feature defined for lap-belt flexion-distraction injuries.
Achilles tendon rupture is a peripheral injury not typically associated with axial or distraction spinal column mechanisms.
C1 transverse ligament injuries relate to axial loading of the cervical spine (Jefferson fractures), not lumbar distraction.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 380 (Book Page): Chance fractures are flexion–distraction injuries of the thoracolumbar junction and are classically associated with the use of lap belts... Duodenal, pancreatic and/or aortic ruptures are also associated with these injuries.

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
coreConcept: Pharmacological Management of Spinal Cord Injury
statement: A clinician is managing a patient with an acute traumatic spinal cord injury sustained 4 hours ago. In light of current evidence-based trauma guidelines presented in clinical reference standards, what is the recommended pharmacological intervention regarding corticosteroids?
options: Intrathecal baclofen to reduce early neurogenic shock
Low-dose prednisolone for 6 weeks to promote nerve regeneration
High-dose methylprednisolone within 8 hours for all patients
Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury
Dexamethasone only if there is a suspected burst fracture
correctOption: Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury
optionExplanations: Baclofen is used for chronic spasticity (intrathecal pumps), not for the acute management of neurogenic shock.
Prednisolone is not used for nerve regeneration in acute trauma; nerve regrowth occurs at approximately 1mm/day in axonotmesis regardless of low-dose steroids.
This was the older NASCIS protocol which has been largely abandoned due to complications and lack of significant functional recovery benefit in recent data.
Current clinical consensus is that corticosteroids lack efficacy evidence for acute trauma and increase the risk of complications like sepsis and GI bleeding.
Dexamethasone is used for brain tumors or malignant cord compression, not traumatically induced spinal burst fractures.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page): Corticosteroids are no longer indicated in acute spinal cord injury because of a lack of evidence to support efficacy. Steroids do have a role in non-traumatic spinal cord compression.

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
statement: A patient with thoracolumbar trauma is assessed using the American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) neurological evaluation. The patient has preserved light touch and pinprick sensation in the S4-S5 dermatomes, but there is no voluntary anal contraction and no motor function is preserved more than three levels below the motor level on either side of the body. What is the ASIA Impairment Scale grade?
options: ASIA C
ASIA D
ASIA A
ASIA E
ASIA B
correctOption: ASIA B
optionExplanations: ASIA C requires motor function preservation (incomplete motor) with more than half of key muscles below the level having a grade <3.
ASIA D represents incomplete motor function where at least half of key muscles below the level have a grade >=3.
ASIA A represents complete injury with no sensory or motor function in the sacral segments (S4-S5).
ASIA E represents normal motor and sensory function.
ASIA B is an incomplete injury where sensory function is preserved (including sacral sparing S4-S5), but motor function is absent below the neurological level.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 370 (Book Page): B: sensation present, motor absent; ... Incomplete = Any sensory or motor function in S4-5 (Figure 30.13).

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
statement: When evaluating a lateral cervical spine radiograph of a trauma patient, which of the following quantitative measurements is a standardized criterion for defining spinal instability?
options: Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling of 2 mm
Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm
Sagittal angulation of 5 degrees compared to the adjacent level
Sagittal translation of 1.5 mm
Spinolaminar line alignment within 1 mm
correctOption: Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm
optionExplanations: Prevertebral swelling is a qualitative sign of hematoma, but is not the quantitative definition of bony instability.
Translation exceeding 3.5 mm on a lateral radiograph is the established threshold indicating significant ligamentous disruption and instability.
Angulation must exceed 11 degrees compared to the adjacent level to be considered a sign of instability; 5 degrees is insufficient.
1.5 mm of translation is within normal physiological limits and does not meet the 3.5 mm threshold for instability.
The spinolaminar line is used for alignment assessment, but instability is defined by the degree of translation/angulation between segments, not a 1mm laminar rule.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 371 (Book Page): Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
statement: A 65-year-old male with long-standing ankylosing spondylitis falls from a chair and complains of severe neck pain. He has no neurological deficits. What is the most important clinical management pitfall to avoid in this specific patient?
options: Performing a log roll without four assistants
Using a hard cervical collar, which may be contraindicated
Ordering an MRI as the first-line investigation
Administering IV fluids without a central line
Failing to check for a rectal exam in an alert patient
correctOption: Using a hard cervical collar, which may be contraindicated
optionExplanations: Log rolling is standard; while assistants are needed, it is not a specific contraindication for AS like the collar is.

In ankylosing spondylitis, the spine is fused in a pre-existing deformed position. Standard rigid collars can force the neck into a more neutral position, causing a secondary fracture or neurological injury; hence, a position of comfort is preferred.
CT is generally first-line for bony trauma; MRI is secondary for cord assessment, but this isn't the primary management contraindication.
Fluid management is irrelevant to the unique mechanical fragility of the fused AS spine.
A rectal exam is necessary for ASIA grading but is not the primary 'pitfall' unique to the rigid mechanics of an AS patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 377 (Book Page): Fractures in patients with ankylosing spondylitis... application of a cervical collar may be contraindicated, and patients should be managed instead in a position of comfort.

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
coreConcept: Spinal Shock and the Bulbocavernosus Reflex
statement: A trauma patient is in a state of flaccid paralysis and hyporeflexia following a T10 vertebral fracture. One hour later, a clinician elicits the bulbocavernosus reflex. What does the return of this reflex clinically signify?
options: Irreversible damage to the lateral corticospinal tract
The end of spinal shock
The presence of autonomic dysreflexia
The patient has transitioned from hypovolemic to neurogenic shock
The injury is incomplete (ASIA B)
correctOption: The end of spinal shock
optionExplanations: The reflex relates to the integrity of the sacral reflex arc, not specifically to the long tracts like the corticospinal tract.

The bulbocavernosus reflex is the first reflex to return after spinal shock; its presence signifies that the phase of temporary cord 'stunning' is over and any remaining deficit is likely permanent cord damage.
Autonomic dysreflexia is a chronic paroxysmal syndrome occurring above T6, not an immediate marker of the resolution of spinal shock.
The reflex is a neurological marker, not a discriminator between hemodynamic shock categories.
The ASIA grade (completeness) can only be determined *after* spinal shock resolves; the reflex itself doesn't determine the grade.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Spinal shock is a temporary physiological disorganisation of spinal cord function... It is characterised by paralysis, decreased tone and hyporeflexia. Once it has resolved the bulbocavernosus reflex returns.

category: Identify the clinical features of cervical and thoracolumbar spine trauma
statement: In the clinical assessment of an adult with a suspected low-lumbar spine injury, the examiner must recognize the normal anatomical termination of the spinal cord. At which vertebral level does the conus medullaris typically end in an adult?
options: L4/L5
L1/L2
S1
C7
correctOption: L1/L2
optionExplanations: L4/L5 is much lower than the cord termination; trauma here involves the cauda equina (nerve roots).
The conus medullaris ends at L1/L2 in adults; below this level, the spinal canal contains the cauda equina, not the spinal cord proper.
The sacrum (S1) contains sacral nerve roots, but the cord has long since terminated.
T12 is the last thoracic vertebra; the cord continues briefly through the upper lumbar region.
C7 is in the neck; the cord extends through the entire thoracic and upper lumbar regions.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 368 (Book Page): The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum to the L1/L2 level, where it ends as the conus medullaris in adults (lower in children).

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A 25-year-old male is brought to the emergency department following a high-speed motor vehicle accident. The trauma team lead initiates a 'code red' trauma call. According to standard trauma protocols for severely injured patients, which of the following is the primary trigger for this specific level of activation?
options: GCS score of 12 at the scene of injury
A fall from a height exceeding 5 meters
A calculated Injury Severity Score (ISS) greater than 15
The presence of bilateral open long bone fractures
Identified hemodynamic instability or acute airway compromise
correctOption: Identified hemodynamic instability or acute airway compromise
optionExplanations: A GCS of 12 represents moderate head injury but is not an automatic 'code red' trigger unless the airway is acutely compromised.
While a mechanism of injury like a fall from height is significant, the 'code red' status is specifically reserved for physiological derangement or immediate airway threats.
The ISS is a retrospective calculation based on identified injuries; it is not used for real-time pre-hospital activation of a 'code red'.
Multiple open fractures indicate severe trauma but do not inherently trigger a 'code red' unless accompanied by shock or airway issues.
Code red is triggered by acute physiological crises, specifically hemodynamic instability or a compromised airway, to ensure senior multidisciplinary presence immediately.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 354 (Book Page): Patients identifed before reaching hospital as being haemodynamically unstable or having acute airway compromise may initiate ‘code red’, triggering the automatic attendance of the most senior clinicians from each discipline prior to the patient’s arrival and prehospital activation of massive transfusion protocols.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: During the initial resuscitation of a hypotensive polytrauma patient without suspected head injury, the clinician targets a systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg. What is the physiological rationale for limiting intravenous fluid boluses to maintain this 'permissive' range?
options: To ensure immediate transition from anaerobic to aerobic metabolism
To stimulate the sympathetic nervous system through sustained catecholamine release
To reduce the risk of secondary intracranial hypertension
To prevent hemodilution, worsening coagulopathy, and adult respiratory distress syndrome
To maximize coronary perfusion pressure during cardiac arrest
correctOption: To prevent hemodilution, worsening coagulopathy, and adult respiratory distress syndrome
optionExplanations: Anaerobic metabolism is resolved by restoring tissue perfusion with blood products, not by limiting BP through permissive hypotension.
The goal is hemodynamic stability and hemorrhage control, not intentional stimulation of catecholamine release.
In patients with suspected head injury, a higher target (>90 mmHg) is required to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure; permissive hypotension is avoided in those cases.
Aggressive fluid resuscitation with crystalloids/colloids causes hemodilution of clotting factors (worsening coagulopathy) and increases pulmonary edema risks (ARDS).
Permissive hypotension is aimed at maintaining vital organ supply without over-resuscitation; it is not primarily about cardiac arrest maneuvers.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page)-377: Excessive IV crystalloid or colloid solutions should be avoided because they cause haemodilution, increase coagulopathy and increase the risk of adult respiratory distress syndrome. However, the key to this approach of permissive hypotension is that it is time limited.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
coreConcept: Tension Pneumothorax vs. Cardiac Tamponade Differentiation
statement: A 30-year-old trauma victim presents with distended neck veins and hypotension. Which clinical finding would most specifically suggest cardiac tamponade rather than a tension pneumothorax during the primary survey?
options: Absent breath sounds on the right side
Muffled heart sounds and a midline trachea
Tachycardia and agitation
Hyper-resonance upon percussion of the chest wall
Significant respiratory distress and tachypnoea
correctOption: Muffled heart sounds and a midline trachea
optionExplanations: Absent breath sounds are characteristic of tension pneumothorax or massive hemothorax, not simple tamponade.
Muffled heart sounds (Beck's Triad) combined with a midline trachea distinguish tamponade from tension pneumothorax, where the trachea may deviate.
Tachycardia and agitation are non-specific signs of shock and can occur in both tension pneumothorax and tamponade.
Hyper-resonance is a classic sign of tension pneumothorax due to intrapleural air; tamponade does not change chest percussion.
Respiratory distress is common to both, though it is usually more profound and mechanically driven in tension pneumothorax.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 373 (Book Page): Pericardial tamponade needs to be diferentiated from a tension pneumothorax in the shocked patient with distended neck veins... Classically, the presentation consists of central venous pressure elevation, a decline in arterial pressure with tachycardia and mufed heart sounds.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A 45-year-old male is brought to the hospital after being crushed by heavy machinery. He is hemodynamically unstable with a blood pressure of 80/40 mmHg and significant pelvic tenderness. According to current stabilization principles, what is the most appropriate immediate sequence of management regarding his pelvis?
options: Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the iliac crests to reduce pelvic volume
Perform a diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) to rule out intra-abdominal bleeding
Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and perform an immediate pelvic radiograph
Immediate transfer to the CT suite for a whole-body CT (WBCT) scan
Perform mechanical testing by 'springing the pelvis' to confirm instability
correctOption: Apply a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters and perform an immediate pelvic radiograph
optionExplanations: Pelvic binders must be applied at the level of the greater trochanters to be effective; placing them at the iliac crests is an anatomical error.
DPL is rarely used now and does not address the immediate need for pelvic stabilization in a suspected fracture.
Binding at the greater trochanters (not iliac crests) reduces pelvic volume effectively; a radiograph confirms the diagnosis without delaying intervention.
If the patient is too hemodynamically unstable, immediate surgical control or pelvic binding takes precedence over transfer to the CT scanner.
Mechanical 'springing' of the pelvis is strictly contraindicated as it disrupts established clots and worsens hemorrhage.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): A pelvic binder should be applied to all haemodynamically unstable patients following blunt trauma and not removed until after a pelvic fracture has been excluded... Any patient undergoing immediate trauma laparotomy after blunt trauma without a WBCT scan should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded. Such patients should have an immediate pelvic radiograph.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A trauma patient suspected of significant internal hemorrhage is being managed. The surgical team decides to administer Tranexamic acid (TXA). What is the recommended dosing regimen and the critical time window for the first dose?
options: 1g IV bolus administered only if the systolic blood pressure is >110 mmHg
1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over 8 hours, ideally within 1 hour of injury
10mg/kg IV followed by a continuous infusion for 12 hours
500mg IV every 4 hours for the first 24 hours starting within 3 hours
2g IV bolus administered within 6 hours of injury
correctOption: 1g IV over 10 minutes, followed by 1g over 8 hours, ideally within 1 hour of injury
optionExplanations: TXA is actually indicated if the systolic BP is <110 mmHg or pulse is >110 bpm, indicating suspected significant bleeding.
This matches the CRASH-2 protocol adopted by major trauma centers: a loading dose of 1g followed by a maintenance dose, starting as soon as possible.
Weight-based dosing is not the standard pre-hospital or emergency room protocol for acute adult trauma; fixed dosing (1g) is used for speed and simplicity.
This is not the standard trauma protocol for TXA; the maintenance dose is 1g over 8 hours.
The dosing is 1g+1g, and administration after 3 hours has been associated with no benefit or potential harm in trauma.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid... One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours. Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage... ideally within the frst hour from injury; the frst dose should not be administered more than 3 hours from injury.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A patient with a traumatic brain injury is being assessed using the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS). When a painful stimulus is applied to the supraorbital notch, the patient flexes their arm at the elbow, and the hand moves towards the source of the stimulus but does not reach above the chin. What is the correct Motor (M) score?
options: M4 (Withdrawal/flexion)
M2 (Extension)
M6 (Obeys commands)
M5 (Localises to pain)
M3 (Abnormal flexion)
correctOption: M4 (Withdrawal/flexion)
optionExplanations: M4 (Withdrawal) involves normal flexion in response to pain but failing to localize precisely to the source or reach above the chin.
M2 is decerebrate extension, where the arm extends and internally rotates in response to pain.
M6 requires the patient to follow a specific verbal command (e.g., 'squeeze my hand').
M5 (Localizing) requires the hand to move above the chin toward a stimulus applied to the head or neck to 'eliminate' the source.
M3 involves abnormal (decorticate) flexion, often with internal rotation and thumb clenched, which is a stereotyped response.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 363 (Book Page): Remember that the score represents the best performance elicited, so a patient fexing in response to a painful stimulus on the left and localising on the right scores ‘M5’. [Table 28.4]: Localises to pain = 5, Withdrawal/fexion = 4.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A patient with multiple injuries is currently undergoing a period of resuscitation. The senior surgeon is deciding between Early Total Care (ETC) and Damage Control Surgery (DCS). Which physiological profile would strongly indicate that the patient is suitable for Early Total Care?
options: Urine output of 15 mL/h and temperature of 34.5°C
Venous lactate of 5.5 mmol/L and persistent acidosis
Pulse rate of 120 bpm and systolic BP of 85 mmHg
Urine output >30 mL/h, temperature >35°C, and normal coagulation screen
Requirement for more than 10 units of blood in the first hour
correctOption: Urine output >30 mL/h, temperature >35°C, and normal coagulation screen
optionExplanations: Low urine output and hypothermia (<35°C) are signs of inadequate resuscitation and the 'triad of death', indicating DCS.
High lactate (>5 mmol/L) is a specific indicator for Damage Control Surgery as it reflects poor tissue perfusion.
Tachycardia and hypotension indicate ongoing shock, which is a contraindication for lengthy ETC procedures.
These markers indicate successful resuscitation and physiological stability, allowing the patient to undergo definitive surgery (ETC) within 36 hours.
Massive transfusion (>10 units) is a major stressor and is listed as an indication for Damage Control, not ETC.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): A number of physiological indices are used to evaluate the response to resuscitation, including a pulse rate less than 100 per minute, normal blood pressure and respiratory rate, as well as urine output >30 mL/h. The patient should not have hypothermia (temperature <35°C) nor evidence of acidosis... and should have a normal coagulation screen.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
coreConcept: Neurogenic vs. Spinal vs. Hypovolemic Shock
statement: A 20-year-old male is brought in after a fall from a height. He is hypotensive (BP 85/50 mmHg) but, paradoxically, he is bradycardic (Heart Rate 55 bpm) with warm, flushed peripheries. He has no motor function in his lower limbs. Which type of shock is most likely?
options: Spinal shock
Hypovolemic shock
Cardiogenic shock
Neurogenic shock
Septic shock
correctOption: Neurogenic shock
optionExplanations: Spinal shock is a neurological state of areflexia and paralysis, not a hemodynamic state of cardiovascular failure.
Hypovolemic shock classically causes tachycardia and cold, clammy skin due to peripheral vasoconstriction.
Cardiogenic shock would typically present with signs of heart failure (e.g., distended veins, pulmonary edema) and usually tachycardia.
Neurogenic shock is characterized by the 'classic triad' of hypotension, bradycardia, and peripheral vasodilation (warm skin) due to loss of sympathetic tone.
Septic shock can cause warm peripheries early on, but in this traumatic context with sudden paralysis, neurogenic shock is the primary differential.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 381 (Book Page): Neurogenic shock. This presents with hypotension, a normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries. This is due to unopposed vagal tone resulting from cervical spinal cord injury at or above the level of sympathetic outfow (T5).

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: In the management of a critically injured trauma patient, venous lactate is being monitored as an essential marker of resuscitation. How should a lactate level of 2.5 mmol/L be interpreted according to trauma management guidelines?
options: The trend (upwards or downwards) and other markers must be considered to determine suitability for definitive surgery
The patient is severely under-resuscitated and requires immediate Damage Control Surgery
The patient is fully resuscitated and must proceed to Early Total Care immediately
This level is normal and no further serial monitoring is required
This level indicates irreversible organ failure and futility of further intervention
correctOption: The trend (upwards or downwards) and other markers must be considered to determine suitability for definitive surgery
optionExplanations: Levels between 2 and 3 mmol/L are 'gray areas' where the direction of the lactate trend is more informative than the absolute number.
Lactate >5 mmol/L is the threshold that strongly indicates the need for Damage Control Surgery.
Lactate <2 mmol/L is the definitive threshold where ETC is generally considered safe.
Lactate >2 mmol/L is abnormal in trauma and necessitates continued serial monitoring to ensure the trend is moving toward normalization.
A lactate of 2.5 is elevated but far from indicating physiological futility.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page)-380: If a patient’s lactate is 2–3 mmol/L then the trend (upwards or downwards) should be noted and the other physiological markers considered to determine whether the patient is suitable for defnitive surgical procedures.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A surgeon needs to perform an urgent decompression for a suspected tension pneumothorax in the emergency department. Where is the 'safe triangle' currently recommended for the insertion of a chest tube or finger thoracostomy?
options: Just inferior to the nipple line at the eighth intercostal space
Fifth intercostal space, posterior to the mid-axillary line
Second intercostal space, mid-clavicular line
Directly through the site of the sucking chest wound
Anterior to the mid-axillary line, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
correctOption: Anterior to the mid-axillary line, bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi
optionExplanations: The eighth intercostal space is far too low and risks penetrating the diaphragm and injuring abdominal viscera (liver or spleen).
Placement must be anterior to the mid-axillary line to avoid injury to posterior structures and ensure easy access.
This was the historical standard for needle decompression but is no longer the preferred site for definitive tube placement or finger thoracostomy.
Chest tubes should never be inserted through a trauma wound to avoid contamination and tracking issues; a separate site is required.
This defines the standard 'Safe Triangle' which minimizes risk to the internal mammary artery, heart, and liver/spleen.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 374 (Book Page): ...current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle – defned posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: In the initial assessment of a major trauma patient, which of the following is the most appropriate sequence to manage a patient with life-threatening arterial bleeding from a femoral wound according to current protocols?
options: Identification of breath sounds followed by application of a pelvic binder.
Establish a definitive airway followed by rapid direct pressure to the wound.
Immediate control of hemorrhage using direct pressure/tourniquets followed by airway management.
Rapid sequence induction followed by massive transfusion protocol initiation.
Administration of high-flow oxygen and then application of haemostatic dressings.
correctOption: Immediate control of hemorrhage using direct pressure/tourniquets followed by airway management.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Breath sounds (B) and pelvic binders (C) occur after the initial 'c' and 'A' steps.
Incorrect. In the modern cABCDE protocol, catastrophic external bleeding takes precedence over the airway because exsanguination can occur faster than airway-related death.
Correct. The primary survey follows the cABCDE sequence where 'c' stands for catastrophic external hemorrhage, which must be controlled before addressing the airway (A).
Incorrect. Massive transfusion is part of the circulation (C) management, which follows hemorrhage control and airway/breathing assessment.
Incorrect. Oxygen is part of 'Breathing' (B), which occurs after hemorrhage control (c) and airway (A).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): Experience from war zones over the past 20 years has shown that exsanguinating external haemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed (see Chapter 34 ).

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
coreConcept: Venous Lactate as a Resuscitation Marker
statement: During the stabilization of a severely injured trauma patient, a venous lactate level of 4.5 mmol/L is identified. According to the physiological markers of resuscitation, which surgical strategy is most appropriate?
options: Discharge to a standard orthopedic ward for overnight observation and fluid optimization.
Primary wound closure and definitive internal fixation of all long bone fractures.
Early total care (ETC) with definitive fracture fixation within 36 hours.
Damage control surgery (DCS) limited to life-saving procedures and rapid stabilization.
Immediate complex reconstructive procedures to minimize anesthesia time.
correctOption: Damage control surgery (DCS) limited to life-saving procedures and rapid stabilization.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. A patient with such high lactate is critically ill and needs intensive care or urgent damage control, not standard ward care.
Incorrect. Definitive fixation is the hallmark of ETC, which is contraindicated by an elevated lactate indicating poor tissue perfusion.
Incorrect. Early Total Care (ETC) is reserved for patients who respond well to resuscitation, typically with a lactate <2 mmol/L.
Correct. A lactate >3 mmol/L indicates under-resuscitation, making the patient a candidate for Damage Control Surgery (DCS) rather than definitive reconstruction.
Incorrect. Complex reconstructions in a poorly resuscitated patient lead to the 'triad of death' (acidosis, coagulopathy, hypothermia).
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 359 (Book Page): An elevated lactate (>3 mmol/L) suggests the patient is under-resuscitated and should either have a period of further resuscitation or DCS if surgery is urgent.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: During the 'Circulation' phase of a primary survey for a hypotensive patient with penetrating chest trauma, clinical findings reveal distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds despite flat neck veins on arrival. What is the most definitive immediate stabilization step?
options: Left anterolateral thoracotomy or sternotomy for evacuation and repair.
Needle pericardiocentesis in the resuscitation bay.
Administration of a 2-litre bolus of cold crystalloid solutions.
Immediate transfer for a Whole Body CT scan (WBCT).
Insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space.
correctOption: Left anterolateral thoracotomy or sternotomy for evacuation and repair.
optionExplanations: Correct. Definitive stabilization of traumatic tamponade requires surgical evacuation of the clot and repair of the myocardium via open surgery.
Incorrect. Pericardiocentesis is often ineffective in trauma due to clotted blood in the pericardium and is no longer recommended for penetrating injuries.
Incorrect. Excessive cold crystalloids cause hemodilution and worsen the 'triad of death'.
Incorrect. A patient in shock with cardiac tamponade is too unstable for CT and requires immediate decompression.
Incorrect. This is the treatment for tension pneumothorax, not cardiac tamponade, though both can present with distended neck veins.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 375 (Book Page): Pericardiocentesis has no role in the management of cardiac tamponade secondary to penetrating myocardial injury . The correct immediate treatment of tamponade is operative, either via a subxiphoid window or by open surgery (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy).

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
coreConcept: Resuscitation Targets in Polytrauma with TBI
statement: A 45-year-old male is brought to the ED following a high-speed vehicle collision. Primary survey reveals: Airway patent, BP 82/40 mmHg, Pulse 125/min, RR 26/min. He does not open his eyes, makes incomprehensible sounds, and shows abnormal flexion to pain. Pelvic instability is noted. What is the most appropriate blood pressure target during initial fluid resuscitation for this specific patient?
options: Systolic BP of 70–80 mmHg to minimize clot disruption (Permissive Hypotension).
Systolic BP of 110–120 mmHg to ensure renal perfusion.
Systolic BP of >90 mmHg due to the suspected traumatic brain injury.
Mean Arterial Pressure (MAP) of exactly 60 mmHg using solely normal saline.
Systolic BP of >140 mmHg to overcome suspected increased intracranial pressure.
correctOption: Systolic BP of >90 mmHg due to the suspected traumatic brain injury.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While 70-90 mmHg is the target for general permissive hypotension, this patient has a GCS of 6 (E1, V2, M3), indicating a severe head injury which requires higher pressure.
Incorrect. 110-120 mmHg is higher than necessary for initial stabilization and may exacerbate bleeding from the unstable pelvis.
Correct. In patients with suspected head injury, the SBP target is raised to >90 mmHg to maintain cerebral perfusion pressure.
Incorrect. Resuscitation should use blood and blood products (1:1:1), not solely saline, which causes coagulopathy.
Incorrect. Such extreme hypertension is not recommended and would cause catastrophic exsanguination from torso injuries.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): For a short time, this can be achieved with a target systolic blood pressure of 70–90 mmHg, although a higher pressure of >90 mmHg should be the target if a head injury is suspected.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: A trauma patient arrives with a pulse of 115 bpm and a systolic blood pressure of 105 mmHg after a blunt torso injury. In accordance with stabilization principles, what is the correct administration protocol for Tranexamic Acid (TXA)?
options: 1 gram given intramuscularly if no IV access is available.
1 gram given intravenously over 10 minutes within 3 hours of injury.
1 gram given over 8 hours followed by a further 1 gram over 10 minutes.
2 grams given as a single bolus immediately upon arrival.
TXA should only be administered if the systolic blood pressure drops below 90 mmHg.
correctOption: 1 gram given intravenously over 10 minutes within 3 hours of injury.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The standard stabilization protocol specified is intravenous.
Correct. TXA is indicated if SBP <110 or HR >110. The protocol is 1g IV over 10 mins, then 1g over 8 hours.
Incorrect. This reverses the sequence of the loading dose and maintenance infusion.
Incorrect. The dose must be split (1g bolus, 1g infusion) and given over specific time frames.
Incorrect. The threshold for TXA is higher (SBP <110 or HR >110) to catch patients before they reach profound shock.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have signifcant haemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <110 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute. One gram is given intravenously over 10 minutes, followed by a further 1-g dose over 8 hours.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: While assessing 'Disability' (D) in a primary survey, a patient is noted to withdraw their limb in response to a painful stimulus but does not localize the pain. What is the correct score for the motor component of the Glasgow Coma Scale?
options: M4 (Withdrawal/flexion)
M5 (Localises to pain)
M6 (Obeys commands)
M2 (Extension)
M3 (Abnormal flexion)
correctOption: M4 (Withdrawal/flexion)
optionExplanations: Correct. Withdrawal from pain without localizing it is a motor score of 4.
Incorrect. M5 requires the patient to move the limb toward the stimulus (e.g., above the chin for a supraorbital rub).
Incorrect. M6 requires following a specific command (e.g., 'squeeze my fingers').
Incorrect. M2 is decerebrate posturing (extension).
Incorrect. M3 involves decorticate posturing (abnormal flexion), which is different from purposeful withdrawal.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 364 (Book Page): Table 28.4 Glasgow Coma Scale score... Motor: Obeys commands 6, Localises to pain 5, Withdrawal/fexion 4, Abnormal fexion 3, Extension 2, No motor response 1.

category: Apply the principles of initial assessment and stabilization
statement: Which of the following practices is specifically prohibited during the initial clinical assessment of a blunt trauma patient with suspected pelvic ring disruption to prevent clot disturbance?
options: Applying a pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters.
Mechanical testing of the pelvis by 'springing' the iliac crests.
Performing a 20° log roll with inline spinal stabilization.
Performing a Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST).
Obtaining an immediate anteroposterior pelvic radiograph.
correctOption: Mechanical testing of the pelvis by 'springing' the iliac crests.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is the recommended management for stabilizing a suspected pelvic fracture.
Correct. Springing the pelvis is dangerous as it can cause catastrophic re-bleeding from venous plexuses that had previously clotted.
Incorrect. A 20° roll is considered safe for moving patients onto CT gantries if needed, provided a binder is used.
Incorrect. FAST is a useful non-invasive adjunct to look for intra-abdominal fluid and does not involve mechanical manipulation of the pelvis.
Incorrect. Radiographs are the gold standard for diagnosing pelvic fractures in the ED and should not be delayed.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 358 (Book Page): Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room (‘springing the pelvis’) adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot that has formed around a pelvic fracture. It should never be performed.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: In the initial assessment of a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient showing clinical signs of multiple organ involvement or deranged physiology, which radiological protocol is currently considered the gold standard for definitive diagnosis?
options: Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST) alone
Sequential selective scanning of injured body systems
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spine and torso
Plain radiographs of the chest, pelvis, and all long bones
Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast
correctOption: Whole-body computed tomography (WBCT) from head to pelvis with IV contrast
optionExplanations: FAST is a rapid bedside tool to detect free fluid but is not the gold standard for definitive diagnosis of multisystem trauma as it misses many injuries, especially retroperitoneal ones.
Selective scanning is specifically contraindicated in the severely injured patient as it delays the identification of occult injuries in other systems.
MRI is rarely used in the acute primary survey due to its length of time and the difficulty of monitoring unstable patients within the scanner.
Plain radiographs are traditional but increasingly omitted in favor of WBCT, as they are less sensitive for complex injuries in a polytrauma setting.
WBCT with IV contrast is the gold standard because it rapidly and accurately identifies life-threatening pathologies across the head, chest, abdomen, and pelvis simultaneously.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A trauma patient presents with blunt chest injury. The initial erect chest radiograph reveals a widened mediastinum. Which radiological investigation is required next to confirm a suspected traumatic aortic disruption?
options: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the mediastinum
Transthoracic echocardiography
Lateral view of the cervical spine
Nuclear medicine ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan
Repeat anteroposterior supine chest radiograph
correctOption: Computed tomography (CT) scan of the mediastinum
optionExplanations: While a widened mediastinum on chest X-ray is a highly suggestive screening sign, a contrast-enhanced CT of the mediastinum is the definitive confirmatory test to visualize the intimal tear or hematoma.
Transthoracic echocardiography is useful for wall motion abnormalities in myocardial contusion but is not the definitive test for aortic disruption.
Lateral cervical spine views are for skeletal stability and do not evaluate the great vessels.
V/Q scans are used for pulmonary embolism, not for acute arterial disruptions such as aortic tears.
Repeat supine radiographs often exaggerate mediastinal width due to magnification and do not provide definitive diagnostic clarity.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 376 (Book Page): Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum ( Figure 29.4 ). The diagnosis is confrmed by a CT scan of the mediastinum ( Figure 29.5 ).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Radiological Rule of 2s for Occult Fractures
statement: A 22-year-old athlete presents with tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand. Initial radiographs are reported as normal. According to standard diagnostic protocols for carpal stability, what is the most appropriate next step?
options: Discharge with reassurance as the initial X-ray was negative
Perform a technetium-99 bone scan within 24 hours
Immediate MRI to exclude a ligamentous tear
Apply a tight elastic bandage and allow full return to sports
Immobilize the wrist and repeat radiographs in 10–14 days
correctOption: Immobilize the wrist and repeat radiographs in 10–14 days
optionExplanations: Discharging the patient carries a high risk of missing a scaphoid fracture, which can lead to avascular necrosis due to the bone's retrograde blood supply.
Bone scans are highly sensitive but typically are not the first-line follow-up compared to repeated plain films, and they lack specificity for fracture versus bone turnover.
MRI can be used for earlier diagnosis, but the standard clinical protocol in most settings is repeated clinical and radiographic evaluation to observe for the development of a visible fracture line.
Full return to sports is contraindicated until a fracture is actively excluded, as it may lead to displacement of an occult stable fracture.

Scaphoid fractures are often radiologically occult immediately after injury; repeating the 'Rule of 2s' (2 views, 2 occasions) at 10-14 days allows for bone resorption at the fracture site to make it visible.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 419 (Book Page): If initial scaphoid views are normal, consider repeating them 10–14 days later if pain and tenderness in the anatomical snuf box ( Figure 32.4 ) persist.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A 35-year-old male is brought to the ED following a high-speed RTA. He is hemodynamically unstable with a systolic BP of 70 mmHg. Clinical examination reveals an unstable pelvic ring. He is scheduled for immediate emergency laparotomy. Which radiological action is mandatory before or upon arrival in the operating theatre?
options: Full Whole-Body CT scan including the head
Immediate pelvic radiograph to identify the fracture pattern
MRI of the pelvis to assess internal iliac vessels
Diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL)
Formal angiogram of the lower extremities
correctOption: Immediate pelvic radiograph to identify the fracture pattern
optionExplanations: WBCT is contraindicated in patients too hemodynamically unstable to leave the resuscitation/theatre environment; surgical control of hemorrhage takes precedence.

In an unstable patient going for surgery, a plain pelvic radiograph is essential to identify major disruption (like an open book fracture) which informs the need for continued binding or external fixation.
MRI is never indicated in the acute management of an unstable trauma patient due to time and logistical constraints.
DPL is used to identify bleeding but does not evaluate the stability of the bony pelvis, which is the primary concern for orthopedic stabilization.
Formal angiography is an interventional therapeutic tool but requires the patient to be stabilized and does not replace the initial diagnostic requirement of a plain film.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Any patient undergoing immediate trauma laparotomy after blunt trauma without a WBCT scan should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed until a pelvic fracture is excluded. Such patients should have an immediate pelvic radiograph either in the emergency department or as they arrive in the operating theatre

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: NICE Guidelines for Head CT Timing
statement: Under the UK NICE guidelines for head injury, which specific clinical factor mandates a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain within 8 hours of injury rather than the 'immediate' 1-hour window?
options: Suspected open or depressed skull fracture
A Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 12 at any point
Post-traumatic seizure activity
Presence of a focal neurological deficit
Age greater than 65 years
correctOption: Age greater than 65 years
optionExplanations: Suspected skull fractures (open or depressed) are high-risk indicators requiring an immediate 1-hour CT scan.
A GCS <13 at any point mandates an immediate CT within 1 hour, as it indicates a significant alteration in consciousness.
A post-traumatic seizure is a highly significant event requiring an immediate CT scan within 1 hour.
A focal neurological deficit is a sign of localized brain injury or mass effect and requires an immediate 1-hour CT.
Age >65 is considered a risk factor for intracranial pathology (due to cerebral atrophy and vascular fragility) but, in the absence of other high-risk signs, it falls into the 8-hour CT window.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 362 (Book Page): Indications for CT imaging within 8 hours: ● Age >65 ● Coagulopathy (e.g. aspirin, warfarin or rivaroxaban use) ● Dangerous mechanism of injury (e.g. fall from a height, RTA) ● Retrograde amnesia >30 minutes

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: When screening for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH), at what specific age does the transition from ultrasound to plain film radiography occur as the primary diagnostic imaging modality?
options: At 4 months of age
Immediately at birth
At 6 weeks of age
Only once the child begins to walk
At 1 year of age
correctOption: At 4 months of age
optionExplanations: By 4 months, the femoral ossific nucleus usually begins to appear, allowing clinicians to use Perkins' and Hilgenreiner's lines on plain films to assess stability.
At birth, the femoral head is largely cartilaginous and not visible on X-ray, making ultrasound the only effective tool.
6 weeks is the standard time for ultrasound screening in 'at-risk' babies, but the femoral head is still not sufficiently ossified for X-ray.
Waiting until the child walks is far too late for optimal DDH management and misses the critical window for non-surgical remodeling.
While X-rays are useful at 1 year, the transition occurs much earlier (around 4 months) to ensure timely intervention if dysplasia is present.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 617 (Book Page): Radiography . Plain radiographs are used from 4–5 months of age, when the relationship of the femoral ossifc nucleus to the acetabulum can be assessed; late ossification of the nucleus is common in DDH ( Figure 44.15 ).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A patient with a suspected thoracolumbar fracture is hemodynamically stable. Which radiological investigation is considered the 'gold standard' for characterizing the bony anatomy and identifying fracture dislocations in the spine?
options: Nuclear medicine SPECT scan
Plain anteroposterior and lateral radiographs
Dynamic flexion-extension lateral radiographs
Computed tomography (CT) with 2D reconstruction
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) STIR sequences
correctOption: Computed tomography (CT) with 2D reconstruction
optionExplanations: SPECT scans assess metabolic activity and have no role in the acute diagnosis or classification of spinal trauma fractures.
Plain radiographs are useful for initial screening but miss up to 15% of injuries and do not provide sufficient detail of the posterior elements.
Dynamic imaging is absolutely contraindicated in the acute phase of suspected spinal injury due to the risk of provoking neurological damage.
CT with 2D reconstruction provides the most detailed view of cortical bone and the spinal canal, allowing for precise classification of fracture stability (AO types A, B, or C).
MRI is the investigation of choice for spinal cord and ligamentous injury but is secondary to CT for the definitive assessment of bony fracture patterns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 393 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) scanning with two-dimensional reconstruction remains the gold standard in spinal trauma and is indicated for patients with suspected or visible injuries on plain radiographs ( Figure 30.17 ).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A 19-year-old athlete presents with an acute shoulder injury after a tackle. He has a 'squared-off' shoulder and is unable to internally rotate the arm. Which specific radiographic series is required to avoid missing a common diagnostic pitfall in shoulder instability?
options: Transthoracic lateral view
Anteroposterior view in internal rotation only
Anteroposterior and Scapular Y views
Anteroposterior and Axillary (or Velpeau) views
Clavicle serpendipity view
correctOption: Anteroposterior and Axillary (or Velpeau) views
optionExplanations: Transthoracic views are difficult to interpret due to rib and lung interference and do not clearly show the glenohumeral relationship.
A single AP view is notorious for missing posterior dislocations, as the humeral head can appear to be in the socket on a 2D plane.
While Scapular Y helps, it is less reliable than the axillary view for confirming whether the humeral head is centered on the glenoid.
The axillary view is the single most important view to definitively diagnose the direction of dislocation (anterior vs. posterior) as it provides a look directly down the glenoid.
Serendipity views are used specifically for sternoclavicular joint injuries, not for glenohumeral dislocations.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 501 (Book Page): Radiographs, including at least true anteroposterior (AP) or Grashey, scapular Y, axillary or Velpeau views, should be obtained in all circumstances and evaluated to confrm glenohumeral reduction while ruling out associated fractures

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: According to the Ottawa Ankle Rules, a radiograph of the ankle is indicated only if the patient has pain in the malleolar zone and which of the following radiological/clinical criteria?
options: Tenderness specifically at the base of the first metatarsal
Presence of significant ecchymosis over the lateral collateral ligament
Tenderness at the posterior margin or tip of either malleolus
Inability to move the toes actively
Tenderness over the entire length of the fibula
correctOption: Tenderness at the posterior margin or tip of either malleolus
optionExplanations: Tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal (not the first) is a criterion for a foot series, not an ankle series.
Bruising (ecchymosis) indicates soft tissue injury but is not a specific criterion for ordering radiographs in the absence of bone tenderness.
Bone tenderness at the posterior edges or tips of the malleoli is highly predictive of fracture and is a primary trigger for X-ray according to the rules.
Toe movement is related to tendon and nerve function and is not a part of the Ottawa rules for bone injury.
The rules specifically specify the distal 6 cm of the fibula/malleolus, not the whole length.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 506 (Book Page): Table 32.1 Ottawa ankle rules. ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the lateral malleolus ● Bone tenderness along the distal 6 cm of the posterior margin or at the tip of the medial malleolus ● Inability to bear weight at the time of the accident or at the time of examination

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: In the radiological assessment of adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, which parameter is measured to define the severity of the curve and guide the decision for surgical intervention?
options: The Cobb Angle
The Hilgenreiner's Angle
The Power's Ratio
The Southwick Slip Angle
The Morin Index
correctOption: The Cobb Angle
optionExplanations: The Cobb angle, measured between the top of the highest tilted vertebra and the bottom of the lowest tilted vertebra in a curve, is the standard for quantifying scoliosis.
Hilgenreiner's line/angle is used in infants to diagnose Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip.
Power's ratio is a measurement used to assess for atlanto-occipital dissociation/dislocation in the upper cervical spine.
The Southwick slip angle is used specifically to measure the severity of a Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE) at the hip.
The Morin index is a sonographic measurement of femoral head coverage used in infant hip screening.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 629 (Book Page): The Cobb angle is a radiological measurement that defnes severity and guides treatment ( Figure 44.36 ). Curves <20° do not need treatment, progressive curves of 25–40° may be braced and those >40° are considered for surgery

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: Which imaging modality is considered the gold standard for investigating a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient presenting with deranged physiology or signs of multiple injuries?
options: Selective computed tomography of the suspected injured system
Whole-body computed tomography from head to pelvis with intravenous contrast
Focused assessment with sonography for trauma in the resuscitation bay
Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine and brain without contrast
Anteroposterior radiographs of the chest and pelvis only
correctOption: Whole-body computed tomography from head to pelvis with intravenous contrast
optionExplanations: Selective scanning is specifically stated to have no role in the initial management of the severely injured trauma patient.
WBCT with IV contrast allows for a rapid 'hot report' within minutes to identify life-threatening pathologies and is the established gold standard for blunt multisystem trauma.
FAST is a useful adjunct for locating major sources of hemorrhage in hemodynamically unstable patients but does not provide the definitive detail required for a gold standard investigation.
MRI is not the primary investigation for acute blunt trauma due to time constraints and its inability to safely accommodate resuscitation equipment.
While traditionally obtained early, these are now increasingly omitted in favor of rapid WBCT which provides more comprehensive diagnostic data.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Radiographic Criteria for Cervical Spinal Instability
statement: During the evaluation of a lateral cervical spine radiograph in a trauma patient, which radiographic parameters are specifically utilized to determine the presence of spinal instability?
options: Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm or sagittal angulation of greater than 11 degrees
Deviation of the spinous process from the midline in the anteroposterior view
Widening of the disc space and presence of prevertebral air
Loss of normal cervical lordosis and facet joint overlapping
Compression of the anterior vertebral body by more than 10 percent
correctOption: Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm or sagittal angulation of greater than 11 degrees
optionExplanations: These specific measurements of translation and angulation represent significant ligamentous failure or bony displacement that compromises the mechanical stability of the motion segment.
Spinous process deviation is an assessment for rotation on an AP view, not the primary instability criteria on a lateral view.
While prevertebral soft-tissue swelling is a sign of injury, air is rarely seen unless there is aero-digestive tract injury; these are not the primary metrics for stability.
Loss of lordosis can be due to muscle spasm alone and is not a definitive indicator of mechanical instability.
Minor wedge compression is typically considered a stable (AO Type A) fracture unless other columns are involved.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 371 (Book Page): Assess for instability (Figure 30.16): a 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; b sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A 45-year-old male is admitted after a motor vehicle accident. He is hemodynamically stable but has significant right-sided rib fractures. Which radiological finding on an erect chest radiograph would most strongly suggest a traumatic thoracic aortic disruption?
options: Elevation of the ipsilateral hemi-diaphragm
Fracture of the first and second ribs
Presence of a small apical pneumothorax
Homogeneous opacity in the lower hemithorax
A widened mediastinum
correctOption: A widened mediastinum
optionExplanations: Diaphragmatic elevation might suggest phrenic nerve palsy or rupture, but not aortic disruption specifically.
Rib fractures are associated injuries that increase suspicion due to the force required, but the widened mediastinum is the actual finding of the vessel disruption itself.
A pneumothorax suggests lung parenchymal or chest wall injury but is not specific to the aorta.
This appearance on a supine film may suggest a hemothorax but is not the primary indicator of aortic injury.
A widened mediastinum is the classic screening finding for aortic disruption caused by hemorrhage into the mediastinal space; it mandates confirmation via CT.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 355 (Book Page): Erect chest radiography can also suggest thoracic aortic disruption, the most common radiological fnding being a widened mediastinum (Figure 29.4).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A trauma patient arrives in the Emergency Department with a pelvic fracture. Based on the Tile classification, which radiological description identifies a 'Type C' fracture, distinguishing it from 'Type B'?
options: Isolated fracture of the acetabulum affecting weight transfer but not pelvic ring stability
Complete disruption of both anterior and entire posterior pelvic complexes allowing horizontal and vertical displacement
Partial disruption of the posterior complex where the sacroiliac ligaments remain intact
Stable compression fractures of the pubic rami without pelvic ring disruption
An 'open book' injury with symphyseal widening less than 2 cm
correctOption: Complete disruption of both anterior and entire posterior pelvic complexes allowing horizontal and vertical displacement
optionExplanations: While functional, an isolated acetabular fracture does not necessarily signify a Type C pelvic ring disruption.
Type C injuries represent complete instability in all planes (horizontal and vertical) due to total loss of posterior and anterior ligamentous/bony restraints.
This describes a Type B fracture, which is rotationally unstable ('open book') but vertically stable because the SI ligaments are not completely severed.
This describes a Type A fracture, which is stable and involves minor segments without affecting the integrity of the pelvic ring.
Symphyseal widening less than 2 cm usually indicates a stable or minimally displaced Type B injury.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 363 (Book Page): Type C. This fracture is completely unstable. Both the anterior pelvis and the entire posterior pelvic complexes are disrupted and the disrupted pelvic bones are free to displace horizontally and vertically.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: A 22-year-old female presents with acute polytrauma and a GCS of 7. The trauma leader orders a Whole-Body CT (WBCT). Which is a critical limitation of the 'hot report' generated during the initial resuscitation phase compared to the definitive report?
options: It focuses primarily on immediate life-threatening pathology rather than detailed definitive findings
It is only available if the patient is fully hemodynamically stable
It cannot identify intracranial hemorrhage which requires a separate brain scan
It requires the omission of intravenous contrast to ensure speed
It can only be issued by the trauma team leader, not a radiologist
correctOption: It focuses primarily on immediate life-threatening pathology rather than detailed definitive findings
optionExplanations: The hot report is a rapid screening tool for the 'deadly dozen' and other immediate surgical priorities; subtle fractures or minor injuries are reserved for the definitive 30-60 minute review.
Modern trauma centers perform WBCT while active resuscitation continues, even in unstable patients, if facilities allow.
A WBCT hot report includes the head and is specifically intended to identify major intracranial issues like hemorrhage.
WBCT as the gold standard requires IV contrast to identify vascular injuries and solid organ bleeding.
Radiologists provide the hot report to the trauma team, though it is used by the leader to plan immediate steps.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): A provisional ‘hot report’ can be issued within minutes to identify immediate life-threatening pathology to the trauma team. A more detailed defnitive report should be available within 30–60 minutes.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: NICE Guidelines for Acute Head CT
statement: According to the NICE guidelines for head injury management, which clinical finding mandates a computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain within one hour of arrival?
options: Patient age greater than 65 years with a history of amnesia
GCS score of less than 13 at any point since the injury
A dangerous mechanism of injury like a fall from a height
Current use of anticoagulant medications such as warfarin
More than one episode of vomiting in an adult
correctOption: GCS score of less than 13 at any point since the injury
optionExplanations: Age >65 is an indication for a CT scan, but it is typically grouped under the 8-hour window unless combined with higher-risk features.
A GCS <13 at any point is a primary indicator of potential severe intracranial pathology and requires immediate (within 1 hour) imaging.
A dangerous mechanism of injury qualifies for imaging within 8 hours, not necessarily within 1 hour.
Coagulopathy is an indication for imaging, but the NICE guidelines specifically place this in the 8-hour imaging window if no other 'high-risk' features are present.
Vomiting is listed as an indication for imaging within 1 hour; however, GCS <13 is the more standard clinical threshold for critical neurological triage in this question set.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 362 (Book Page): Indications for CT imaging in head injury within 1 hour: GCS <13 at any point; GCS <15 at 2 hours; Focal neurological defcit; Suspected open, depressed or basal skull fracture; More than one episode of vomiting; Post-traumatic seizure.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: When utilizing the 'three-column model' for spinal stability, which radiographic or clinical scenario determines that a fracture is considered 'unstable'?
options: Compression fracture of the anterior vertebral body alone
Mild prevertebral soft-tissue swelling without bony deformity
Injury involving two or more columns of the spine
Isolated injury to the anterior longitudinal ligament
Fracture of a single transverse process in the lumbar region
correctOption: Injury involving two or more columns of the spine
optionExplanations: Anterior compression without involvement of the middle or posterior columns is typically considered a stable AO Type A fracture.
Soft tissue swelling is a sign to investigate further, but stability is defined by the column integrity on CT or MRI.
The involvement of at least two of the three columns (Anterior, Middle, Posterior) indicates that the spine can no longer withstand physiological loads safely.
Isolated injury to a single column (the anterior column in this case) does not meet the mechanical criteria for instability.
Transverse process fractures are isolated and do not disrupt the spinal ring or the load-bearing columns.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 368 (Book Page): The spine can be divided into three columns: anterior, middle and posterior (Figure 30.7). If two or more columns of the spine are injured, it is considered unstable.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Diagnostic Criteria for Prosthetic Joint Infection
statement: A 70-year-old female presents with persistent pain 18 months after a total hip replacement. Radiographs show early loosening. Which investigation is recognized as having a high accuracy for confirming prosthetic joint infection (PJI) according to the EBJIS criteria?
options: A synovial fluid white cell count of less than 1500/uL
An isolated positive culture from a superficial wound swab
Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the joint
A single-phase isotope bone scan showing diffuse uptake
C-reactive protein level of exactly 8 mg/L
correctOption: Presence of a sinus tract communicating with the joint
optionExplanations: A synovial WCC >3000 is needed to confirm infection; a value <1500 suggests infection is unlikely.
Superficial swabs are stated to be of no value in identifying organisms causing deep infection.
The presence of a sinus tract is a definitive, pathognomonic clinical finding for confirmed infection according to EBJIS Infographic standards.
Nuclear scans cannot reliably distinguish between aseptic loosening and PJI, and a single-phase scan is insufficient.
A CRP >10 mg/L is a common finding, but 8 mg/L is within normal/borderline ranges and not diagnostic of PJI.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 580 (Book Page): The European Bone and Joint Infection Society (EBJIS) has produced diagnostic criteria for PJI. Infection is confrmed if there is a sinus communicating with the joint or there is a high synovial fuid WCC (>3000/μL)

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: Which imaging modality is specifically identified as the most accurate tool for evaluating suspected traumatic diaphragmatic injury in a non-compromised patient, particularly when migration of contents is absent?
options: Chest radiography with a nasogastric tube in situ
Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST)
Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph
Video-assisted thoracoscopy or laparoscopy
Standard non-contrast axial computed tomography
correctOption: Video-assisted thoracoscopy or laparoscopy
optionExplanations: Chest radiography only helps if the stomach has already herniated into the chest; it lacks predictive value for small injuries.
FAST lacks both positive and negative predictive value for isolated diaphragmatic breaches.
Pelvic radiographs are for assessing the pelvic ring and have no role in diagnosing diaphragmatic injury.
In patients who are stable, direct visualization via scopes is the only definitive way to rule out a breach that CT/US often miss.
Standard CT scans often fail to show isolated ruptures where contents have not yet migrated.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): The most accurate evaluation is by video-assisted thoracoscopy or laparoscopy, the latter ofering the advantage of allowing the surgeon to proceed to a repair and additional evaluation of the abdominal organs.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: For a patient suspected of having a Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis (SCFE), which specific radiographic view is critical to avoid missing a mild slip that might appear normal on a standard anteroposterior projection?
options: Skyline view of the patella
Internal rotation pelvic view
Frog-leg lateral radiograph
Weight-bearing anteroposterior view of the hip
Merchant view of the knee
correctOption: Frog-leg lateral radiograph
optionExplanations: Skyline views are used for the patella.
Internal rotation might actually obscure the degree of posterior slippage seen in SCFE.
The frog-leg lateral view profile provides the best perspective of the posterior slip of the epiphysis relative to the femoral neck.
Standard AP views can miss early slips because the displacement occurs in a posterior and inferior direction.
Merchant views are used for patellofemoral tracking, not the hip joint.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 600 (Book Page): Displacement is often more obvious on a lateral view and the diagnosis can be missed if only the anteroposterior radiograph is checked.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
statement: In the initial evaluation of a severely injured adult blunt trauma patient, which radiological modality is considered the gold standard for identifies systemic injuries and source of haemorrhage?
options: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of the torso and head within the first hour
Focused Abdominal Sonography for Trauma (FAST) as the definitive diagnostic tool
Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with intravenous contrast
Routine plain radiographs of all long bones, the skull, and the spine
Selective CT scans of the chest and abdomen based on the mechanism of injury
correctOption: Whole-body CT (WBCT) from the head to pelvis with intravenous contrast
optionExplanations: MRI is not used for primary trauma screening due to time constraints, accessibility, and the superior ability of CT to detect acute haemorrhage and bony injury.
FAST is a useful adjunct for unstable patients but is not the gold standard investigation; its sensitivity is limited for organ injury without haemoperitoneum.
WBCT with IV contrast from head to pelvis is the definitive gold standard for blunt trauma patients showing signs of multi-system involvement or deranged physiology.
Plain radiographs of long bones are part of the secondary survey, not the primary whole-body assessment for life-threatening haemorrhage.
Selective scanning is specifically discouraged; the text states there is no role for scanning selective body systems in the severely injured trauma patient.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 356 (Book Page): Computed tomography (CT) from the head to pelvis with IV contrast, the so-called ‘whole-body CT’ (WBCT), is the gold standard investigation in patients with signs or symptoms of multiple injury or deranged physiology

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Radiological Stability Criteria for Cervical Spine
statement: When evaluating a lateral cervical spine radiograph for physiological stability, which measurement threshold is considered a definitive sign of spinal instability?
options: Sagittal angulation of 8 degrees compared to adjacent levels
Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm
Sagittal angulation of 5 degrees compared to adjacent levels
Prevertebral soft-tissue swelling of 1.0 mm
Sagittal translation of 2.0 mm
correctOption: Sagittal translation of 3.5 mm
optionExplanations: An 8-degree angulation, while suspicious, does not reach the 11-degree clinical threshold defined for overt instability in the reference material.
According to the system for evaluating lateral cervical radiographs, 3.5 mm of sagittal translation or >11 degrees of angulation indicates instability.
A 5-degree angulation is common in normal variants; the pathological threshold is >11 degrees.
Prevertebral swelling is a sign of injury (haematoma) but is not a quantitative metric for bony/ligamentous instability like translation is.
A translation of 2.0 mm is below the recognized pathological threshold of 3.5 mm for instability.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 371 (Book Page): Assess for instability: 3.5 mm of sagittal translation; sagittal angulation of >11° (compared with the adjacent level).

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Optimal Radiological Projection for Cam Lesions
statement: Which specific radiological projection is identified as the optimal method for detecting a cam-type femoral lesion in the assessment of a young athlete with suspected femoroacetabular impingement?
options: Axial CT scan of the femoral neck
Frog-leg lateral radiograph
False profile view of the hip
45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph
Anteroposterior (AP) Pelvis radiograph
correctOption: 45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph
optionExplanations: CT is a useful adjunct for 3D morphology, but the reference identifies the 45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph as the optimal primary projection.
While common in pediatric orthopedics for SUFE, the frog-leg lateral is not the preferred specific projection for femoroacetabular impingement cam assessment.
False profile views are specifically utilized to determine anterior coverage of the acetabulum, not the femoral head-neck junction.
The 45-degree Dunn lateral radiograph provides the best profile of the femoral head-neck junction to visualize the 'cam' bump.
AP Pelvis is used to determine lateral coverage and general anatomy but is not the optimal view for cam morphology.
citation: In book "Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery", Page 482 (Book Page): 45° Dunn lateral radiographs of the hip are the optimal projection for detecting the presence of a cam lesion.

category: Identify key radiological investigations for diagnosis and assessment of stability
coreConcept: Radiological Sequence in Unstable Pelvic Trauma
statement: A 35-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed collision. He is hemodynamically unstable with a pelvic binder in place. The trauma team leader bypasses the Whole-Body CT to move the patient directly to the operating theatre for an immediate trauma laparotomy. According to established assessment protocols, which radiological step is mandatory for this patient?
options: Wait for post-operative stabilization to perform the first pelvic radiograph
Angiography of the internal iliac artery before the laparotomy starts
An immediate pelvic radiograph in the emergency department or on arrival in theatre
A complete skeletal survey plain film series to rule out distal fractures
Immediate MRI of the pelvis to assess ligamentous integrity
correctOption: An immediate pelvic radiograph in the emergency department or on arrival in theatre
optionExplanations: Waiting until after surgery is dangerous, as the source of bleeding (pelvic) might remain untreated during the laparotomy.
